INCLUDE a record if it satisfies:

1. At least one substantive CLIMATE-RELATED component

AND

2. At least one qualifying HEALTH, MITIGATION, or ADAPTATION component.

A record does NOT need to contain a human health outcome if it qualifies through the mitigation or adaptation pathways.

--------------------------------------------------
1. CLIMATE-RELATED COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

A record has a climate-related component if it substantively addresses one or more of the following:

A. Climate change or climate variability

B. Climate/weather variables, such as:
- temperature
- precipitation
- humidity
- wind
- drought
- heat
- cold
- other weather or climate conditions

C. Climate-related extreme events, such as:
- heatwaves
- floods
- droughts
- storms
- hurricanes/cyclones
- storm surges
- wildfires
- other climate-related hazards

D. Fossil fuels or fossil-fuel use, including:
- extraction
- production
- combustion
- consumption
- replacement
- their greenhouse-gas or other climate-forcing emissions (NOT non-climate combustion pollutants such as PAHs or heavy metals — see the air-pollution rule below)

E. Greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents, including:
- methane
- carbon dioxide
- nitrous oxide
- black carbon
- other recognized climate-forcing agents

F. An intervention or action that changes emissions of greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents.

A climate-related component is substantive when the climate-related factor, event, agent, or emission is:
- measured;
- analyzed;
- modeled;
- used as an exposure;
- used as an outcome;
- affected by an intervention; or
- otherwise important to the research question.

The climate-related component does NOT need to be the main topic of the paper.

For example:
- An animal nutrition study that evaluates methane emissions can have a climate-related component because methane is a climate-forcing agent.
- An air-pollution study can have a climate-related component when it studies a recognized climate-forcing pollutant/agent.
- A flood model can have a climate-related component when it studies a climate-related flood hazard.

DO NOT consider a record climate-related merely because climate change, temperature, fossil fuels, greenhouse gases, or another climate-related term appears incidentally in the background, introduction, discussion, or references.

IMPORTANT:
Air pollution in general is NOT automatically a climate-related component. The climate criterion is satisfied only when the pollutant is itself a relevant climate-forcing agent or the record explicitly connects the pollution to climate change.

IMPORTANT — INTENT:
A greenhouse gas, climate-forcing agent, or fossil-fuel substance makes a record climate-related ONLY when the study concerns it as a climate, energy, emissions, or air-quality matter. It does NOT qualify when the substance is present for an unrelated reason, e.g.: a greenhouse gas studied as a drug or toxicant (recreational nitrous-oxide abuse); a single fossil-fuel-derived chemical studied only for cellular/clinical toxicology (a diesel-exhaust compound tested in vitro); fossil-fuel infrastructure studied only as an industrial-accident or safety hazard (a pipeline explosion). The agent must be substantive to the research question as a climate/energy/emissions matter, not merely named.

--------------------------------------------------
2. QUALIFYING HEALTH COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The health pathway is satisfied when the record addresses human health or health systems, including:

- disease
- illness
- clinical symptoms
- morbidity
- mortality
- injury
- respiratory or cardiovascular health
- human exposure
- health risks
- occupational health
- public health
- healthcare
- health services
- health-system capacity, preparedness, resilience, or functioning

A record qualifies through the health pathway when the climate-related factor/event/agent/fossil fuel is studied in relation to human health or health systems.

Do NOT require a climate-related extreme event if a climate-forcing agent, fossil fuel, or other qualifying climate-related factor is directly related to human health.

For example:
A study measuring atmospheric pollutants and examining respiratory health can qualify through the climate + health pathway when the pollutants include relevant climate-forcing agents.

Do NOT infer human-health relevance merely because an environmental condition, pollutant, animal disease, agricultural outcome, or ecosystem change could theoretically affect human health.

INDIRECT HEALTH VIA CLIMATE EXPOSURE PATHWAYS (CCHE):
The health component is ALSO satisfied when the record substantively addresses a recognised climate-health exposure pathway through which climate/weather or a climate-forcing agent affects human health, even without a named clinical outcome. The recognised pathways are:
- Air quality (particulate matter, ground-level ozone, wildfire smoke/haze, pollen/aeroallergens, dust storms) -> respiratory/cardiovascular disease;
- Extreme weather events (floods, droughts, storms, storm surges, coastal flooding) -> injuries, fatalities, mental-health effects, health-care disruption;
- Food supply and safety / food security -> undernutrition, foodborne disease;
- Heat stress (heatwaves, cold spells, UV exposure) -> heat-related illness, skin/eye damage;
- Social factors (climate-driven displacement, migration, conflict) -> physical and mental-health effects;
- Vector distribution and ecology (mosquitoes, ticks, rodents, sandflies) -> vector-borne disease (malaria, dengue, Lyme, West Nile, etc.);
- Water quality and quantity (waterborne pathogens, HARMFUL ALGAL BLOOMS / cyanobacteria, drought- or flood-related contamination) -> cholera, cryptosporidiosis, diarrhoeal disease, etc.
A study of one of these exposures in a climate/weather or fossil-fuel/climate-forcing-agent context satisfies the health component through the indirect pathway. This does NOT override the guard above: a merely hypothetical or unstated health link still does not qualify -- the exposure pathway must be a substantive subject of the record.

--------------------------------------------------
3. QUALIFYING MITIGATION COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The mitigation pathway is satisfied when the record studies an action, intervention, technology, practice, policy, or management strategy that is intended to:

- reduce greenhouse-gas emissions;
- reduce another climate-forcing emission;
- remove greenhouse gases;
- reduce fossil-fuel use;
- replace fossil fuels;
- reduce dependence on fossil fuels; or
- otherwise mitigate climate change.

The record does not need to use the word "mitigation".

An intervention that directly changes or reduces emissions of a climate-forcing agent can qualify as mitigation even when the primary subject of the paper is something else.

For example:
A study of dietary sulphur in dairy cattle that examines effects on methane emissions can qualify because:
1. methane is a climate-forcing agent; and
2. an intervention affecting methane emissions constitutes a potential mitigation action.

Merely measuring methane, carbon dioxide, or another greenhouse gas does NOT by itself constitute mitigation.

The record must study an intervention, action, practice, technology, policy, or management approach that affects or is intended to affect emissions or fossil-fuel use.

IMPORTANT — A MITIGATION ACTION, NOT ENABLING RESEARCH:
The record must study, evaluate, or report the mitigation action itself — an intervention, measure, practice, policy, deployment, or management approach that reduces, or is intended to reduce, emissions or fossil-fuel use, or that upscales greenhouse-gas removals. Upstream, basic, or enabling research that merely relates to, characterises, or could inform a low-carbon technology — without itself studying an emission-reducing action or its effect on emissions or fossil-fuel use — does NOT qualify. For example: soil-physics, materials, or component modelling that "supports the design of" a geothermal or other renewable-energy system is enabling research, not a mitigation action; whereas evaluating a feed intervention that reduces methane emissions, or measures that cut a product's manufacturing emissions, IS a mitigation action.

--------------------------------------------------
4. QUALIFYING ADAPTATION COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The adaptation pathway is satisfied when the record addresses:

- climate adaptation;
- preparedness;
- resilience;
- vulnerability reduction;
- climate-risk management;
- risk reduction;
- adaptation planning;
- preparation for climate-related hazards;
- response to climate-related hazards; or
- assessment of future climate-related risks for decision-making.

Adaptation does not have to mean an intervention that has already been implemented.

Research can qualify as adaptation-supporting research when it directly generates evidence needed for:
- adaptation planning;
- future projections;
- climate-risk assessment;
- preparedness;
- resilience planning;
- vulnerability assessment;
- hazard management; or
- risk reduction.

This includes relevant:
- models;
- datasets;
- experiments;
- projections;
- simulations;
- risk assessments;
- engineering studies;
- monitoring studies;
- decision-support tools.

For example:
A study modeling storm surges and compound coastal flooding can qualify if the study explicitly connects the results to future projections, prevention of flood risks, preparedness, resilience, or adaptation planning.

A study generating experimental data on storm surge, wave, or tsunami impacts on coastal structures can qualify when the research is directly relevant to assessment of coastal hazards, resilience, risk reduction, or adaptation planning.

IMPORTANT:
The exclusion for early-stage research applies primarily to immature mitigation/adaptation TECHNOLOGIES or INTERVENTIONS that are not ready for plausible real-world use.

Do NOT exclude ordinary scientific research, modeling, experiments, or data-generation merely because they are not themselves an implemented adaptation action.

IMPORTANT — ADAPTATION PURPOSE:
The adaptation pathway requires the record to frame its purpose, explicitly or by direct inference, as informing human or societal climate adaptation, preparedness, resilience, or climate-risk management. The following do NOT qualify on their own: physiological/biological acclimation of organisms to temperature (the organism adapting is not climate-adaptation research); routine drainage, civil-engineering, or infrastructure studies with no stated climate-risk or adaptation purpose; descriptions of an ecosystem's protective function without a stated adaptation, risk-reduction, or resilience purpose. "Resilience", "vulnerability", or "adaptation" used in a biological or generic-engineering sense does not satisfy this pathway.

IMPORTANT -- ADAPTATION MUST PROTECT HUMAN HEALTH, HEALTH SYSTEMS, OR HUMAN-IMPORTANT ECOSYSTEMS:
The adaptation pathway is satisfied ONLY when the action or supporting research is intended to reduce the exposure or vulnerability of human health, health systems, or ecosystems of importance to humans (e.g. pollinators, protective or food-producing ecosystems) to actual or expected climate hazards -- typically a hazard that acts on humans through one of the recognised climate-health exposure pathways (air quality, extreme weather, food security, heat, social factors, vectors, water). Adaptation or resilience of purely physical, industrial, or economic assets with no human-health, health-system, or human-important-ecosystem target does NOT qualify. For example: protecting or optimising energy systems or industrial infrastructure against climate variability, or protecting land/soil from erosion, is out of scope unless the record connects it to human health, health systems, or a human-important ecosystem. Protecting human settlements or populations from coastal flooding, storm surge, or other extreme-weather hazards DOES qualify (extreme-weather exposure pathway).

--------------------------------------------------
5. STRENGTH OF THE CONNECTION
--------------------------------------------------

Distinguish between a substantive connection and a merely possible connection.

INCLUDE when the qualifying connection is:

A. EXPLICIT:
The abstract directly states the climate, health, mitigation, or adaptation relationship.

OR

B. DIRECTLY INFERABLE:
The relationship follows directly from what the study measures, evaluates, models, or changes.

For example:
- An intervention changes methane emissions -> mitigation is directly inferable.
- A climate-forcing pollutant is associated with respiratory symptoms -> climate + health is directly inferable.
- A coastal flood model is explicitly intended to inform future risk prevention -> adaptation relevance is explicit.

EXCLUDE when the connection is merely speculative or hypothetical.

For example:
- A generic environmental study that could potentially be useful for climate adaptation but does not indicate any adaptation, climate-risk, future-projection, resilience, or preparedness purpose.
- A pollutant study where the pollutant is not a climate-forcing agent and no climate connection is stated.
- A study of animal health where a human-health implication is merely possible.

--------------------------------------------------
6. ANIMAL STUDIES
--------------------------------------------------

Animal studies are not automatically excluded.

INCLUDE an animal study if it has a qualifying connection to:
- climate mitigation;
- climate adaptation;
- human food security; or
- human health.

Animal health alone is not equivalent to human health.

For example:
An animal nutrition study that evaluates methane emissions can qualify through the climate mitigation pathway even if it has no human-health outcome.

--------------------------------------------------
7. SEASONAL VARIATION
--------------------------------------------------

EXCLUDE records that report only normal seasonal variation without a connection to:
- climate change;
- altered or unusual patterns;
- climate variability;
- climate-related hazards;
- climate impacts;
- mitigation; or
- adaptation.

Do not exclude a record merely because it contains seasonal data if the study also addresses a qualifying climate-related question.

--------------------------------------------------
8. EXCLUSIONS
--------------------------------------------------

EXCLUDE records that:

1. Have no substantive climate-related component.

2. Have a climate-related component but no qualifying health, mitigation, or adaptation component.

3. Mention climate change, climate variables, fossil fuels, or climate-forcing agents only incidentally.

4. Concern normal seasonal variation without an altered, unusual, climate-change, climate-variability, mitigation, or adaptation component.

5. Describe subclinical outcomes that do not manifest as clinical symptoms, unless they are directly relevant to an otherwise qualifying human-health exposure or health risk.

6. Are animal studies with no qualifying climate mitigation, adaptation, human food-security, or human-health connection.

7. Describe an early-stage mitigation/adaptation technology or intervention with no plausible real-world application or deployment.

IMPORTANT:
Do not exclude a record merely because:
- climate change is not the primary topic;
- human health is not the primary topic;
- the study is environmental science, engineering, agriculture, animal science, hydrology, or air pollution research;
- the study is observational;
- the study is computational or modeling-based;
- the study generates experimental data;
- the adaptation action itself has not yet been implemented.

--------------------------------------------------
9. POSITIVE CALIBRATION EXAMPLES
--------------------------------------------------

Example 1:
"Significance of dietary sulphur and sulphate reducing bacteria in lactating dairy cattle"

Decision: INCLUDE

Reason:
The abstract discusses methane gas emissions in relation to an animal-nutrition intervention. Methane is a climate-forcing agent, and an intervention affecting methane emissions can constitute climate mitigation. The primary topic does not need to be climate change or human health.

Example 2:
"Acute effects of air pollution on respiratory health of 50-70 yr old adults"

Decision: INCLUDE

Reason:
The study measures atmospheric pollutants, including relevant climate-forcing pollutants, and directly examines respiratory health. This satisfies the climate + health pathway. A climate-related extreme event, mitigation action, or adaptation action is not additionally required.

Example 3:
"Impact of Tides and Surges on Fluvial Floods in Coastal Regions"

Decision: INCLUDE when the record explicitly connects the modeling to future projections, prevention of flood risks, preparedness, resilience, or adaptation planning.

Reason:
The study addresses a climate-related coastal flooding hazard and produces modeling evidence relevant to future risk management/adaptation. An implemented adaptation intervention is not required.

Example 4:
"Loading and Structural Response of Developed Shorelines Under Waves, Surge, and Tsunami Overland Flow Hazards"

Decision: INCLUDE when the record explicitly connects the research to coastal hazard assessment, risk reduction, resilience, preparedness, or adaptation planning.

Reason:
Experimental or data-generating research can qualify as adaptation-supporting research. The study does not need to implement an adaptation intervention or measure a health outcome.

--------------------------------------------------
10. FINAL DECISION
--------------------------------------------------

Before deciding, ask:

1. What is the substantive climate-related component?
2. Which qualifying pathway applies: health, mitigation, or adaptation?
3. Is that connection explicit or directly inferable from the study?
4. Is the connection substantive rather than merely incidental or hypothetical?

If the answer to question 1 is yes AND at least one qualifying pathway in question 2 is supported by the record, output:

INCLUDE

Otherwise output:

EXCLUDE

Return only the classification:

INCLUDE

or

EXCLUDE

document.name: Spatial-temp oral distribution of fish assemblages in the upstreams of Huangpu River and Suzhou Creek

content.abstract: Fish assemblages were investigated at four sites in the upper reaches of Huangpu River and Suzhou Creek, Shanghai, China monthly between June 2005 and May 2006. Forty four fish species in total, belonging to 10 orders, 14 families, 35 genera, were recorded. A total of 30 species belonging to 6 orders, 10 families and 25 genera, were recorded at Baihe and Huangdu on Suzhou Creek, and a total of 39 species belonging to 10 orders, 13 families and 32 genera were collected at Dianfeng and Songpu Bridge on the Huangpu River. Spatio-temporal distribution patterns were observed for the diversity of fish assemblages, with greater species richness in summer and autumn than in winter and spring, and higher species diversity in the upper Huangpu River than in Suzhou Creek. The fish community at Baihe was highly similar to those at the two sites in the Huangpu River, whereas the fish community at Huangdu station was moderately dissimilar to those at the two Huangpu River sites. Between-stream variation in community composition was greater than within-stream variation. Fish communities at the four sites were dominated by omnivore species, which occupied 51.5-62.5% of the communities, and sedentary species. Songpu Bridge had the highest species richness of river-sea migratory species and river-lake migratory species. The results suggested that the fish assemblages at the four sites are somewhat spatially isolated. Further, water quality and interconnectedness of waterways may be important factors influencing diversity of fish species in upper Suzhou creek. It was suggested that higher species diversity of fish in the upstream section of Huangpu River was due to a larger volume of water body, better interconnectedness of waterways and water quality.

document.name: Resilience of international oil trade networks under extreme event shock-recovery simulations

content.abstract: With the frequent occurrence of black swan events, global energy security situation has become increasingly complex and severe. Assessing the resilience of the international oil trade network (iOTN) is crucial for evaluating its ability to withstand extreme shocks and recover thereafter, ensuring energy security. We overcome the limitations of discrete historical data by developing a simulation model for extreme event shock-recovery in the iOTNs. We introduce network efficiency indicator to measure oil resource allocation efficiency and evaluate network performance. Then, we construct a resilience index to explore the resilience of the iOTNs from dimensions of resistance and recoverability. Our findings indicate that extreme events can lead to sharp declines in performance of the iOTNs, especially when economies with significant trading positions and relations suffer shocks. The upward trend in recoverability and resilience reflects the self-organizing nature of the iOTNs, demonstrating its capacity for optimizing its own structure and functionality. Unlike traditional energy security research based solely on discrete historical data or resistance indicators, our model evaluates resilience from multiple dimensions, offering insights for global energy governance systems while providing diverse perspectives for various economies to mitigate risks and uphold energy security.

document.name: Spreading Depolarization as a Therapeutic Target in Severe Ischemic Stroke: Physiological and Pharmacological Strategies

content.abstract: Background: Spreading depolarization (SD) occurs nearly ubiquitously in malignant hemispheric stroke (MHS) and is strongly implicated in edema progression and lesion expansion. Due to this high burden of SD after infarct, it is of great interest whether SD in MHS patients can be mitigated by physiologic or pharmacologic means and whether this intervention improves clinical outcomes. Here we describe the association between physiological variables and risk of SD in MHS patients who had undergone decompressive craniectomy and present an initial case of using ketamine to target SD in MHS. Methods: We recorded SD using subdural electrodes and time-linked with continuous physiological recordings in five subjects. We assessed physiologic variables in time bins preceding SD compared to those with no SD. Results: Using multivariable logistic regression, we found that increased ETCO2 (OR 0.772, 95% CI 0.655–0.910) and DBP (OR 0.958, 95% CI 0.941–0.991) were protective against SD, while elevated temperature (OR 2.048, 95% CI 1.442–2.909) and WBC (OR 1.113, 95% CI 1.081–1.922) were associated with increased risk of SD. In a subject with recurrent SD, ketamine at a dose of 2 mg/kg/h was found to completely inhibit SD. Conclusion: Fluctuations in physiological variables can be associated with risk of SD after MHS. Ketamine was also found to completely inhibit SD in one subject. These data suggest that use of physiological optimization strategies and/or pharmacologic therapy could inhibit SD in MHS patients, and thereby limit edema and infarct progression. Clinical trials using individualized approaches to target this novel mechanism are warranted.

document.name: Subjective Well-Being, Work Motivation and Organizational Commitment of Chinese Hotel Frontline Employees: A Moderated Mediation Study

content.abstract: Subjective Well-Being, Work Motivation and Organizational Commitment of Chinese Hotel Frontline Employees: A Moderated Mediation Study This study examined the relationships among employee work motivation, subjective well-being (SWB), job enrichment and organizational commitment in a hotel industry context. Based on a thorough literature review, a moderated mediation model was proposed and empirically tested by analyzing 316 survey responses from the frontline hotel employees in Beijing, China. According to regression analyses that examined the mediator role of employee subjective well-being (SWB) and the moderation effect from job enrichment, SWB mediates the paths between the two motivation constructs and organizational commitment, while job enrichment moderates the relationship between work motivation and SWB but not the one between SWB and organizational commitment.

document.name: Removal of Co <sup>2+</sup> Ions in Aqueous Solution via Capacitive Deionization Using a TiO <sub>2</sub> Nanoparticle-Based Electrode

content.abstract: Cobalt contamination from industrial and radioactive sources poses serious environmental and health risks. Conventional removal methods suffer from drawbacks, such as secondary waste generation, high costs, and poor selectivity. Here, we present a capacitive deionization (CDI) system using a TiO<sub>2</sub> nanoparticle-based electrode to utilize their abundant surface hydroxyl groups and strong capability for redox processes. In particular, to enhance the adsorption ability of the electrode, anodized TiO<sub>2</sub> nanoparticles was utilized as an active material of the electrode. The CDI system exhibited a clear trend of enhanced removal performance at higher applied voltage, near-neutral pH (5-7), and lower initial Co<sup>2</sup> <sup>+</sup> concentrations, achieving an excellent maximum removal efficiency of 99.1% under the optimized conditions. This system showed superior removal efficiency from the commercial TiO<sub>2</sub>-based system or the conventional activated carbon-based system, and the removal efficiency was up to 80% under the conditions of coexistence with Na<sup>+</sup>, Ni<sup>2+</sup>, and Zn<sup>2+</sup>. In addition, the system showed about 88% desorption rate with 1 M HCl solution, and the system maintained its removal performance up to 89% in the third cycle. To elucidate the mechanisms underlying this excellent adsorption performance, isotherm and kinetic analyses were conducted, which revealed that the heterogeneous multilayer adsorption governs the reaction, with physical adsorption dominating the initial stage and chemical adsorption prevailing at the later stage. Surface chemical and electrochemical analyses identified three main reactions: Ti-O-Co surface complexation, electrodeposition of Co<sup>0</sup>, and hydrogen evolution reaction-induced Co-(OH)<sub>2</sub> formation. This work establishes TiO<sub>2</sub> NP-based CDI as a highly effective strategy for Co<sup>2</sup> <sup>+</sup> removal, offering exceptional efficiency and broad applicability to critical domains, such as environmental remediation, human health safeguarding, and radioactive wastewater treatment.

attribute.prompt:
You are screening bibliographic records for inclusion in the DESTINY repository, a database aimed at capturing the global literature at the intersection of climate change and health, including relevant climate mitigation and adaptation literature.

Your task is to classify each bibliographic record as exactly one of:

INCLUDE
EXCLUDE

Base your decision only on the title, abstract, and other metadata provided. Do not use outside information to fill gaps in the record.

IMPORTANT:
- Do not require climate change, health, mitigation, or adaptation to be the primary topic of the paper.
- Do not require the paper to use the exact words "climate change", "mitigation", or "adaptation".
- Apply the eligibility criteria to each record independently.
- Do not use an assumed prevalence of relevant records to make the decision.
- If the abstract is missing, very short, garbled, or otherwise incomplete, make the best decision possible from the available information.

CORE DECISION RULE

INCLUDE a record if it satisfies:

1. At least one substantive CLIMATE-RELATED component

AND

2. At least one qualifying HEALTH, MITIGATION, or ADAPTATION component.

A record does NOT need to contain a human health outcome if it qualifies through the mitigation or adaptation pathways.

--------------------------------------------------
1. CLIMATE-RELATED COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

A record has a climate-related component if it substantively addresses one or more of the following:

A. Climate change or climate variability

B. Climate/weather variables, such as:
- temperature
- precipitation
- humidity
- wind
- drought
- heat
- cold
- other weather or climate conditions

C. Climate-related extreme events, such as:
- heatwaves
- floods
- droughts
- storms
- hurricanes/cyclones
- storm surges
- wildfires
- other climate-related hazards

D. Fossil fuels or fossil-fuel use, including:
- extraction
- production
- combustion
- consumption
- replacement
- their greenhouse-gas or other climate-forcing emissions (NOT non-climate combustion pollutants such as PAHs or heavy metals — see the air-pollution rule below)

E. Greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents, including:
- methane
- carbon dioxide
- nitrous oxide
- black carbon
- other recognized climate-forcing agents

F. An intervention or action that changes emissions of greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents.

A climate-related component is substantive when the climate-related factor, event, agent, or emission is:
- measured;
- analyzed;
- modeled;
- used as an exposure;
- used as an outcome;
- affected by an intervention; or
- otherwise important to the research question.

The climate-related component does NOT need to be the main topic of the paper.

For example:
- An animal nutrition study that evaluates methane emissions can have a climate-related component because methane is a climate-forcing agent.
- An air-pollution study can have a climate-related component when it studies a recognized climate-forcing pollutant/agent.
- A flood model can have a climate-related component when it studies a climate-related flood hazard.

DO NOT consider a record climate-related merely because climate change, temperature, fossil fuels, greenhouse gases, or another climate-related term appears incidentally in the background, introduction, discussion, or references.

IMPORTANT:
Air pollution in general is NOT automatically a climate-related component. The climate criterion is satisfied only when the pollutant is itself a relevant climate-forcing agent or the record explicitly connects the pollution to climate change.

IMPORTANT — INTENT:
A greenhouse gas, climate-forcing agent, or fossil-fuel substance makes a record climate-related ONLY when the study concerns it as a climate, energy, emissions, or air-quality matter. It does NOT qualify when the substance is present for an unrelated reason, e.g.: a greenhouse gas studied as a drug or toxicant (recreational nitrous-oxide abuse); a single fossil-fuel-derived chemical studied only for cellular/clinical toxicology (a diesel-exhaust compound tested in vitro); fossil-fuel infrastructure studied only as an industrial-accident or safety hazard (a pipeline explosion). The agent must be substantive to the research question as a climate/energy/emissions matter, not merely named.

--------------------------------------------------
2. QUALIFYING HEALTH COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The health pathway is satisfied when the record addresses human health or health systems, including:

- disease
- illness
- clinical symptoms
- morbidity
- mortality
- injury
- respiratory or cardiovascular health
- human exposure
- health risks
- occupational health
- public health
- healthcare
- health services
- health-system capacity, preparedness, resilience, or functioning

A record qualifies through the health pathway when the climate-related factor/event/agent/fossil fuel is studied in relation to human health or health systems.

Do NOT require a climate-related extreme event if a climate-forcing agent, fossil fuel, or other qualifying climate-related factor is directly related to human health.

For example:
A study measuring atmospheric pollutants and examining respiratory health can qualify through the climate + health pathway when the pollutants include relevant climate-forcing agents.

Do NOT infer human-health relevance merely because an environmental condition, pollutant, animal disease, agricultural outcome, or ecosystem change could theoretically affect human health.

INDIRECT HEALTH VIA CLIMATE EXPOSURE PATHWAYS (CCHE):
The health component is ALSO satisfied when the record substantively addresses a recognised climate-health exposure pathway through which climate/weather or a climate-forcing agent affects human health, even without a named clinical outcome. The recognised pathways are:
- Air quality (particulate matter, ground-level ozone, wildfire smoke/haze, pollen/aeroallergens, dust storms) -> respiratory/cardiovascular disease;
- Extreme weather events (floods, droughts, storms, storm surges, coastal flooding) -> injuries, fatalities, mental-health effects, health-care disruption;
- Food supply and safety / food security -> undernutrition, foodborne disease;
- Heat stress (heatwaves, cold spells, UV exposure) -> heat-related illness, skin/eye damage;
- Social factors (climate-driven displacement, migration, conflict) -> physical and mental-health effects;
- Vector distribution and ecology (mosquitoes, ticks, rodents, sandflies) -> vector-borne disease (malaria, dengue, Lyme, West Nile, etc.);
- Water quality and quantity (waterborne pathogens, HARMFUL ALGAL BLOOMS / cyanobacteria, drought- or flood-related contamination) -> cholera, cryptosporidiosis, diarrhoeal disease, etc.
A study of one of these exposures in a climate/weather or fossil-fuel/climate-forcing-agent context satisfies the health component through the indirect pathway. This does NOT override the guard above: a merely hypothetical or unstated health link still does not qualify -- the exposure pathway must be a substantive subject of the record.

--------------------------------------------------
3. QUALIFYING MITIGATION COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The mitigation pathway is satisfied when the record studies an action, intervention, technology, practice, policy, or management strategy that is intended to:

- reduce greenhouse-gas emissions;
- reduce another climate-forcing emission;
- remove greenhouse gases;
- reduce fossil-fuel use;
- replace fossil fuels;
- reduce dependence on fossil fuels; or
- otherwise mitigate climate change.

The record does not need to use the word "mitigation".

An intervention that directly changes or reduces emissions of a climate-forcing agent can qualify as mitigation even when the primary subject of the paper is something else.

For example:
A study of dietary sulphur in dairy cattle that examines effects on methane emissions can qualify because:
1. methane is a climate-forcing agent; and
2. an intervention affecting methane emissions constitutes a potential mitigation action.

Merely measuring methane, carbon dioxide, or another greenhouse gas does NOT by itself constitute mitigation.

The record must study an intervention, action, practice, technology, policy, or management approach that affects or is intended to affect emissions or fossil-fuel use.

IMPORTANT — A MITIGATION ACTION, NOT ENABLING RESEARCH:
The record must study, evaluate, or report the mitigation action itself — an intervention, measure, practice, policy, deployment, or management approach that reduces, or is intended to reduce, emissions or fossil-fuel use, or that upscales greenhouse-gas removals. Upstream, basic, or enabling research that merely relates to, characterises, or could inform a low-carbon technology — without itself studying an emission-reducing action or its effect on emissions or fossil-fuel use — does NOT qualify. For example: soil-physics, materials, or component modelling that "supports the design of" a geothermal or other renewable-energy system is enabling research, not a mitigation action; whereas evaluating a feed intervention that reduces methane emissions, or measures that cut a product's manufacturing emissions, IS a mitigation action.

--------------------------------------------------
4. QUALIFYING ADAPTATION COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The adaptation pathway is satisfied when the record addresses:

- climate adaptation;
- preparedness;
- resilience;
- vulnerability reduction;
- climate-risk management;
- risk reduction;
- adaptation planning;
- preparation for climate-related hazards;
- response to climate-related hazards; or
- assessment of future climate-related risks for decision-making.

Adaptation does not have to mean an intervention that has already been implemented.

Research can qualify as adaptation-supporting research when it directly generates evidence needed for:
- adaptation planning;
- future projections;
- climate-risk assessment;
- preparedness;
- resilience planning;
- vulnerability assessment;
- hazard management; or
- risk reduction.

This includes relevant:
- models;
- datasets;
- experiments;
- projections;
- simulations;
- risk assessments;
- engineering studies;
- monitoring studies;
- decision-support tools.

For example:
A study modeling storm surges and compound coastal flooding can qualify if the study explicitly connects the results to future projections, prevention of flood risks, preparedness, resilience, or adaptation planning.

A study generating experimental data on storm surge, wave, or tsunami impacts on coastal structures can qualify when the research is directly relevant to assessment of coastal hazards, resilience, risk reduction, or adaptation planning.

IMPORTANT:
The exclusion for early-stage research applies primarily to immature mitigation/adaptation TECHNOLOGIES or INTERVENTIONS that are not ready for plausible real-world use.

Do NOT exclude ordinary scientific research, modeling, experiments, or data-generation merely because they are not themselves an implemented adaptation action.

IMPORTANT — ADAPTATION PURPOSE:
The adaptation pathway requires the record to frame its purpose, explicitly or by direct inference, as informing human or societal climate adaptation, preparedness, resilience, or climate-risk management. The following do NOT qualify on their own: physiological/biological acclimation of organisms to temperature (the organism adapting is not climate-adaptation research); routine drainage, civil-engineering, or infrastructure studies with no stated climate-risk or adaptation purpose; descriptions of an ecosystem's protective function without a stated adaptation, risk-reduction, or resilience purpose. "Resilience", "vulnerability", or "adaptation" used in a biological or generic-engineering sense does not satisfy this pathway.

IMPORTANT -- ADAPTATION MUST PROTECT HUMAN HEALTH, HEALTH SYSTEMS, OR HUMAN-IMPORTANT ECOSYSTEMS:
The adaptation pathway is satisfied ONLY when the action or supporting research is intended to reduce the exposure or vulnerability of human health, health systems, or ecosystems of importance to humans (e.g. pollinators, protective or food-producing ecosystems) to actual or expected climate hazards -- typically a hazard that acts on humans through one of the recognised climate-health exposure pathways (air quality, extreme weather, food security, heat, social factors, vectors, water). Adaptation or resilience of purely physical, industrial, or economic assets with no human-health, health-system, or human-important-ecosystem target does NOT qualify. For example: protecting or optimising energy systems or industrial infrastructure against climate variability, or protecting land/soil from erosion, is out of scope unless the record connects it to human health, health systems, or a human-important ecosystem. Protecting human settlements or populations from coastal flooding, storm surge, or other extreme-weather hazards DOES qualify (extreme-weather exposure pathway).

--------------------------------------------------
5. STRENGTH OF THE CONNECTION
--------------------------------------------------

Distinguish between a substantive connection and a merely possible connection.

INCLUDE when the qualifying connection is:

A. EXPLICIT:
The abstract directly states the climate, health, mitigation, or adaptation relationship.

OR

B. DIRECTLY INFERABLE:
The relationship follows directly from what the study measures, evaluates, models, or changes.

For example:
- An intervention changes methane emissions -> mitigation is directly inferable.
- A climate-forcing pollutant is associated with respiratory symptoms -> climate + health is directly inferable.
- A coastal flood model is explicitly intended to inform future risk prevention -> adaptation relevance is explicit.

For example:
- A generic environmental study that could potentially be useful for climate adaptation but does not indicate any adaptation, climate-risk, future-projection, resilience, or preparedness purpose.
- A pollutant study where the pollutant is not a climate-forcing agent and no climate connection is stated.
- A study of animal health where a human-health implication is merely possible.

Animal health alone is not equivalent to human health.

document.name: Pressurized low polarity water extraction of lignans, proteins and carbohydrates from flaxseed meal

content.abstract:
The physiological benefits of flaxseed against pathological disturbances, such as cancers and heart diseases, are mainly attributed to its high lignan content. This study (Experiment 1) examined the application of pressurized low polarity water (PLPW) for extraction of lignans, proteins and carbohydrates from defatted flaxseed meal. Key processing conditions included temperature (130, 160, 190Â°C), solvent pH (4, 6.5 and 9), solvent to solid ratio (S/S) (90, 150 and 210 mL/g) and introduction of co-packing material (0 and 3 g glass beads). The addition of 3 g glass beads as co-packing material facilitated extraction by enhancing surface contact between the liquid and solid thus shortening extraction time. Elevated temperature accelerated the extraction rate by increasing the solid diffusion coefficient thereby reducing the extraction time. The maximum yield of lignans (99 %) was obtained at temperatures ranging from 160Â°C to 190Â°C, with solvent volume of 180 mL (90 mL/g meal) at pH 9. Optimal conditions for protein extraction (70 %) were pH 9, extraction volume of 420 mL (210 mL/g meal) and 160Â°C. Total carbohydrates yield was maximized at 50% recovery at pH 4 and 160Â°C with 420 mL solvent (210 mL/g meal). Increased temperature accelerated extraction, thus reducing solvent volume and time to reach equilibrium. For the extraction of proteins, however, a temperature of 130-160Â°C is recommended, as proteins are vulnerable to thermal degradation due to heat decomposition. 

The effects of flow rate and geometric dimensions for extraction of lignans and other flaxseed meal bioactives were further investigated in Experiment 2, based on the variables optimized in the previous experiment. Defatted flaxseed meal was extracted with pH 9 buffered water with meal to co-packing glass beads ratio of 1:1.5 at 5.2 MPa (750 psi) and 180Â°C. The aqueous extracts were analyzed for lignan, protein and carbohydrate using HPLC and colorimetric methods. The optimal extraction yields for lignan, protein and carbohydrate were found at flow rates of 1 to 2 mL/min with bed depth between 20 and 26 cm and a S/S ratio of 40 to 100 mL/g. The combination of low flow rate and high bed depth allowed the use of lower S/S ratio with reduced total solvent volume consumption. 

This study also evaluated the mass transfer kinetics governing the process of lignan extraction from flaxseed meal in a fixed bed extraction cell. Diffusion of solute into the continuously flowing solvent was mainly responsible for the mass transfer mechanism as flow rate did not increase proportionally with the yield and rate of extraction. The extraction kinetics were studied on the basis of two approaches: Fickâs diffusion equation and a two-site exponential kinetic model. The proposed two-site exponential kinetic model corresponding to the two-stage extraction (rapid and slow phases) successfully described the experimental data. Diffusivities attained from Fickâs diffusion model ranged from 2 x 10-13 to 9 x 10-13 m2s-1 while mass transfer coefficients were between 4.5 x 10-8 and 2.3 x 10-7 ms-1 for extraction of lignans at 180Â°C, pH 9 with 1:1.5 meal to co-packing material ratio.

content.abstract: Ozone is thought to advance wound healing by inhibiting inflammation, but the mechanism of this phenomenon has not been determined. Although the zebrafish is often used in regeneration experiments, there has been no report of zebrafish treated with ozonated water. We successfully established a zebrafish model of ozonated water treatment and demonstrate that ozonated water stimulates the regeneration of the zebrafish caudal fin, its mechanism, and time dependence. The growth rate of the caudal fin and the number of neutrophils migrating to the caudal fin wound after resection were higher in the experimental (ozonated) group than in the control group, preliminarily confirming that ozone-promoted regeneration is related to the stimulation of an early inflammatory response by ozone. Ozone modulated the expression of tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) in two ways by regulating interleukin 10 (IL-10) expression. Therefore, ozone promotes tissue regeneration by regulating the inflammatory pathways. This effect of ozone in an experimental zebrafish model is demonstrated for the first time, confirming its promotion of wound healing and the mechanism of its effect in tissue regeneration. These results will open up new directions for ozone and regeneration research.

content.abstract: Male heavy smokers were autopsied within 3 days postmortem. Samples from kidney, liver, and lung were taken for analysis of cadmium levels and degree of protein binding within the cytosolic fraction. The levels in lung, liver, and kidney were 0.50 ± 0.35 (X ± SEM), 2.21 ± 0.63, and 17.4 ± 8.8 μg cadmium/g wet weight tissue, respectively. In liver and kidney, approximately 75% was bound to a low-molecular-weight protein whereas the corresponding figure for the lung cytosolic fraction was 56%, a difference being statistically significant (P < 0.05). After concentration of the low-molecular-weight cadmium-binding protein(s) (CdBP) by ultrafiltration and preparative isoelectric focusing in a granulated gel, the cadmium appeared in one single band with pI values of 5.8 (lung and liver) and 6.0 (kidney), respectively. It is therefore concluded that human lung exposed to cadmium, in this case via cigarette smoke, contains a CdBP, which binds cadmium. The relative degree of binding is less in lung than in liver or kidney, implicating that the metal could be more toxic to the lung than to liver or kidney, as the protein probably serves a role in detoxifying cadmium.

--------------------------------------------------
1. CLIMATE-RELATED COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

A record has a climate-related component if it substantively addresses one or more of the following:

A. Climate change or climate variability

B. Climate/weather variables, such as:
- temperature
- precipitation
- humidity
- wind
- drought
- heat
- cold
- other weather or climate conditions

C. Climate-related extreme events, such as:
- heatwaves
- floods
- droughts
- storms
- hurricanes/cyclones
- storm surges
- wildfires
- other climate-related hazards

D. Fossil fuels or fossil-fuel use, including:
- extraction
- production
- combustion
- consumption
- replacement
- their greenhouse-gas or other climate-forcing emissions (NOT non-climate combustion pollutants such as PAHs or heavy metals — see the air-pollution rule below)

E. Greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents, including:
- methane
- carbon dioxide
- nitrous oxide
- black carbon
- other recognized climate-forcing agents

F. An intervention or action that changes emissions of greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents.

A climate-related component is substantive when the climate-related factor, event, agent, or emission is:
- measured;
- analyzed;
- modeled;
- used as an exposure;
- used as an outcome;
- affected by an intervention; or
- otherwise important to the research question.

The climate-related component does NOT need to be the main topic of the paper.

For example:

- An air-pollution study can have a climate-related component when it studies a recognized climate-forcing pollutant/agent.
- A flood model can have a climate-related component when it studies a climate-related flood hazard.

DO NOT consider a record climate-related merely because climate change, temperature, fossil fuels, greenhouse gases, or another climate-related term appears incidentally in the background, introduction, discussion, or references.

IMPORTANT:
Air pollution in general is NOT automatically a climate-related component. The climate criterion is satisfied only when the pollutant is itself a relevant climate-forcing agent or the record explicitly connects the pollution to climate change.

IMPORTANT — INTENT:
A greenhouse gas, climate-forcing agent, or fossil-fuel substance makes a record climate-related ONLY when the study concerns it as a climate, energy, emissions, or air-quality matter. It does NOT qualify when the substance is present for an unrelated reason, e.g.: a greenhouse gas studied as a drug or toxicant (recreational nitrous-oxide abuse); a single fossil-fuel-derived chemical studied only for cellular/clinical toxicology (a diesel-exhaust compound tested in vitro); fossil-fuel infrastructure studied only as an industrial-accident or safety hazard (a pipeline explosion). The agent must be substantive to the research question as a climate/energy/emissions matter, not merely named.

--------------------------------------------------
2. QUALIFYING HEALTH COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The health pathway is satisfied when the record addresses human health or health systems, including:

- disease
- illness
- clinical symptoms
- morbidity
- mortality
- injury
- respiratory or cardiovascular health
- human exposure
- health risks
- occupational health
- public health
- healthcare
- health services
- health-system capacity, preparedness, resilience, or functioning

A record qualifies through the health pathway when the climate-related factor/event/agent/fossil fuel is studied in relation to human health or health systems.

Do NOT require a climate-related extreme event if a climate-forcing agent, fossil fuel, or other qualifying climate-related factor is directly related to human health.

For example:
A study measuring atmospheric pollutants and examining respiratory health can qualify through the climate + health pathway when the pollutants include relevant climate-forcing agents.

Do NOT infer human-health relevance merely because an environmental condition, pollutant, animal disease, agricultural outcome, or ecosystem change could theoretically affect human health.

INDIRECT HEALTH VIA CLIMATE EXPOSURE PATHWAYS (CCHE):
The health component is ALSO satisfied when the record substantively addresses a recognised climate-health exposure pathway through which climate/weather or a climate-forcing agent affects human health, even without a named clinical outcome. The recognised pathways are:
- Air quality (particulate matter, ground-level ozone, wildfire smoke/haze, pollen/aeroallergens, dust storms) -> respiratory/cardiovascular disease;
- Extreme weather events (floods, droughts, storms, storm surges, coastal flooding) -> injuries, fatalities, mental-health effects, health-care disruption;
- Food supply and safety / food security -> undernutrition, foodborne disease;
- Heat stress (heatwaves, cold spells, UV exposure) -> heat-related illness, skin/eye damage;
- Social factors (climate-driven displacement, migration, conflict) -> physical and mental-health effects;
- Vector distribution and ecology (mosquitoes, ticks, rodents, sandflies) -> vector-borne disease (malaria, dengue, Lyme, West Nile, etc.);
- Water quality and quantity (waterborne pathogens, HARMFUL ALGAL BLOOMS / cyanobacteria, drought- or flood-related contamination) -> cholera, cryptosporidiosis, diarrhoeal disease, etc.
A study of one of these exposures in a climate/weather or fossil-fuel/climate-forcing-agent context satisfies the health component through the indirect pathway. This does NOT override the guard above: a merely hypothetical or unstated health link still does not qualify -- the exposure pathway must be a substantive subject of the record.

--------------------------------------------------
3. QUALIFYING MITIGATION COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The mitigation pathway is satisfied when the record studies an action, intervention, technology, practice, policy, or management strategy that is intended to:

- reduce greenhouse-gas emissions;
- reduce another climate-forcing emission;
- remove greenhouse gases;
- reduce fossil-fuel use;
- replace fossil fuels;
- reduce dependence on fossil fuels; or
- otherwise mitigate climate change.

The record does not need to use the word "mitigation".

An intervention that directly changes or reduces emissions of a climate-forcing agent can qualify as mitigation even when the primary subject of the paper is something else.

For example:
A study of dietary sulphur in dairy cattle that examines effects on methane emissions can qualify because:
1. methane is a climate-forcing agent; and
2. an intervention affecting methane emissions constitutes a potential mitigation action.

Merely measuring methane, carbon dioxide, or another greenhouse gas does NOT by itself constitute mitigation.

The record must study an intervention, action, practice, technology, policy, or management approach that affects or is intended to affect emissions or fossil-fuel use.

IMPORTANT — A MITIGATION ACTION, NOT ENABLING RESEARCH:
The record must study, evaluate, or report the mitigation action itself — an intervention, measure, practice, policy, deployment, or management approach that reduces, or is intended to reduce, emissions or fossil-fuel use, or that upscales greenhouse-gas removals. Upstream, basic, or enabling research that merely relates to, characterises, or could inform a low-carbon technology — without itself studying an emission-reducing action or its effect on emissions or fossil-fuel use — does NOT qualify. For example: soil-physics, materials, or component modelling that "supports the design of" a geothermal or other renewable-energy system is enabling research, not a mitigation action; whereas evaluating a feed intervention that reduces methane emissions, or measures that cut a product's manufacturing emissions, IS a mitigation action.

--------------------------------------------------
4. QUALIFYING ADAPTATION COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The adaptation pathway is satisfied when the record addresses:

- climate adaptation;
- preparedness;
- resilience;
- vulnerability reduction;
- climate-risk management;
- risk reduction;
- adaptation planning;
- preparation for climate-related hazards;
- response to climate-related hazards; or
- assessment of future climate-related risks for decision-making.

Adaptation does not have to mean an intervention that has already been implemented.

Research can qualify as adaptation-supporting research when it directly generates evidence needed for:
- adaptation planning;
- future projections;
- climate-risk assessment;
- preparedness;
- resilience planning;
- vulnerability assessment;
- hazard management; or
- risk reduction.

This includes relevant:
- models;
- datasets;
- experiments;
- projections;
- simulations;
- risk assessments;
- engineering studies;
- monitoring studies;
- decision-support tools.

For example:
A study modeling storm surges and compound coastal flooding can qualify if the study explicitly connects the results to future projections, prevention of flood risks, preparedness, resilience, or adaptation planning.

A study generating experimental data on storm surge, wave, or tsunami impacts on coastal structures can qualify when the research is directly relevant to assessment of coastal hazards, resilience, risk reduction, or adaptation planning.

The exclusion for early-stage research applies primarily to immature mitigation/adaptation TECHNOLOGIES or INTERVENTIONS that are not ready for plausible real-world use.

Do NOT exclude ordinary scientific research, modeling, experiments, or data-generation merely because they are not themselves an implemented adaptation action.

IMPORTANT — ADAPTATION PURPOSE:
The adaptation pathway requires the record to frame its purpose, explicitly or by direct inference, as informing human or societal climate adaptation, preparedness, resilience, or climate-risk management. The following do NOT qualify on their own: physiological/biological acclimation of organisms to temperature (the organism adapting is not climate-adaptation research); routine drainage, civil-engineering, or infrastructure studies with no stated climate-risk or adaptation purpose; descriptions of an ecosystem's protective function without a stated adaptation, risk-reduction, or resilience purpose. "Resilience", "vulnerability", or "adaptation" used in a biological or generic-engineering sense does not satisfy this pathway.

IMPORTANT -- ADAPTATION MUST PROTECT HUMAN HEALTH, HEALTH SYSTEMS, OR HUMAN-IMPORTANT ECOSYSTEMS:
The adaptation pathway is satisfied ONLY when the action or supporting research is intended to reduce the exposure or vulnerability of human health, health systems, or ecosystems of importance to humans (e.g. pollinators, protective or food-producing ecosystems) to actual or expected climate hazards -- typically a hazard that acts on humans through one of the recognised climate-health exposure pathways (air quality, extreme weather, food security, heat, social factors, vectors, water). Adaptation or resilience of purely physical, industrial, or economic assets with no human-health, health-system, or human-important-ecosystem target does NOT qualify. For example: protecting or optimising energy systems or industrial infrastructure against climate variability, or protecting land/soil from erosion, is out of scope unless the record connects it to human health, health systems, or a human-important ecosystem. Protecting human settlements or populations from coastal flooding, storm surge, or other extreme-weather hazards DOES qualify (extreme-weather exposure pathway).

--------------------------------------------------

--------------------------------------------------

Distinguish between a substantive connection and a merely possible connection.

INCLUDE when the qualifying connection is:

A. EXPLICIT:
The abstract directly states the climate, health, mitigation, or adaptation relationship.

OR

B. DIRECTLY INFERABLE:
The relationship follows directly from what the study measures, evaluates, models, or changes.

For example:
- An intervention changes methane emissions -> mitigation is directly inferable.
- A climate-forcing pollutant is associated with respiratory symptoms -> climate + health is directly inferable.
- A coastal flood model is explicitly intended to inform future risk prevention -> adaptation relevance is explicit.

- climate variability;
- climate-related hazards;

Do not exclude a record merely because it contains seasonal data if the study also addresses a qualifying climate-related question.

--------------------------------------------------

EXCLUDE records that:

2. Have a climate-related component but no qualifying health, mitigation, or adaptation component.

document.name: The impact of drought in the Karoo - revisiting diatoms as water quality indicators in the upper reaches of the Great Fish River, Eastern Cape, South Africa

content.abstract: This paper examines the efficacy of diatoms as bioindicators of water quality in the upper reaches of the Great Fish River following a period of reduced flow from drought conditions. Of the five sites, three were sampled three times in an 18 month period while the remaining two were sampled once. As a comparison, one headwater site within Mountain Zebra National Park, situated in the same district, was sampled. A total of 166 diatom taxa belonging to 29 genera were identified. Dominant taxa for the Great Fish River were identified as Amphora pediculus; Epithemia sorex; Nitzschia frustulum; Navicula veneta and Craticula buderi. These species, indicative of high nutrient concentrations and moderately saline to brackish conditions can tolerate low flow conditions. The Generic Diatom Index (GDI), the Specific Pollution sensitivity Index (SPI) the Biological Diatom Index (BDI) and the% Pollution Tolerant Valves (%PTV) – part of the UK Trophic Diatom Index (TDI) were used for interpretation of the results. The indices showed that this river is in poor condition. By comparison the headwater site in the Mountain Zebra National Park had Cocconeis placentula var. euglypta, Achnanthidium minutissimum and Cocconeis placentula var. lineata as dominant species and, using the same indices, the river was classified as in moderate to good condition with respect to water quality. When compared to a previous study (2010 – 2012), these sites showed a shift in dominant species indicating a change in water flow conditions and quality.

content.abstract: Introduction:  Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) in patients with skeletal dysplasia is challenging due to the anatomic variances and deformities. The purpose of this review is to understand the technical issues involved in treating these patients.   Methods:  Clinical notes, operative reports, and radiographs were retrospectively reviewed of 12 knees in 8 patients: 3 achondroplasia patients (one with bilateral 10° varus deformities, one with a 30° varus deformity in one knee and 25° varus deformity in the other knee, one with a 14° varus deformity); 3 multiple hereditary exostosis patients (one with bilateral 45° valgus deformities, one with a 45° valgus deformity in one knee and 15° valgus deformity in the other, one with a 11° valgus deformity); and 2 osteogenesis imperfecta patients (one with a 25° varus deformity, one with a 17° valgus deformity).   Results:  Surgical exposure required preoperative placement of soft-tissue expanders to avoid wound complications (1 knee), quadriceps snip (2 knees), and hardware removal (1 knee). Intraoperative balancing of the knee was more complex requiring a lateral epicondylar osteotomy (3 knees), medial release (6 knees), lateral retinacular release (6 knees), and proximal realignment to improve patellar tracking (1 knee). 5 knees required a constrained insert, 2 required tibial augments, one required use of cement and screw technique, and one required modification of an all-polyethylene tibia to accommodate the deformed tibial anatomy. 2 knees required custom tibial components. Complications included 2 peroneal nerve palsies which resolved 3 months postoperatively. Range of motion preoperatively averaged 103° (range 45 to 130°) and 100° postoperatively (range 85 to 120°). All patients were pain-free at their last followup (average follow-up 3.9 years). - Do not require climate change, health, mitigation, or adaptation to be the primary topic of the paper.
- Do not require the paper to use the exact words "climate change", "mitigation", or "adaptation".

- Do not use an assumed prevalence of relevant records to make the decision.
- If the abstract is missing, very short, garbled, or otherwise incomplete, make the best decision possible from the available information.

AND

1. CLIMATE-RELATED COMPONENT

A. Climate change or climate variability

B. Climate/weather variables, such as:
- temperature
- precipitation
- humidity
- wind
- drought
- heat
- cold
- other weather or climate conditions

C. Climate-related extreme events, such as:
- heatwaves
- floods
- droughts
- storms
- hurricanes/cyclones
- storm surges
- wildfires
- other climate-related hazards

D. Fossil fuels or fossil-fuel use, including:
- extraction
- production
- combustion
- consumption
- replacement
- their greenhouse-gas or other climate-forcing emissions (NOT non-climate combustion pollutants such as PAHs or heavy metals — see the air-pollution rule below)

E. Greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents, including:
- methane
- carbon dioxide
- nitrous oxide
- black carbon
- other recognized climate-forcing agents

F. An intervention or action that changes emissions of greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents.

A climate-related component is substantive when the climate-related factor, event, agent, or emission is:
- measured;
- analyzed;
- modeled;
- used as an exposure;
- used as an outcome;
- affected by an intervention; or
- otherwise important to the research question.

The climate-related component does NOT need to be the main topic of the paper.

For example:
- An animal nutrition study that evaluates methane emissions can have a climate-related component because methane is a climate-forcing agent.
- An air-pollution study can have a climate-related component when it studies a recognized climate-forcing pollutant/agent.
- A flood model can have a climate-related component when it studies a climate-related flood hazard.

DO NOT consider a record climate-related merely because climate change, temperature, fossil fuels, greenhouse gases, or another climate-related term appears incidentally in the background, introduction, discussion, or references.

IMPORTANT:
Air pollution in general is NOT automatically a climate-related component. The climate criterion is satisfied only when the pollutant is itself a relevant climate-forcing agent or the record explicitly connects the pollution to climate change.

--------------------------------------------------
2. QUALIFYING HEALTH COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The health pathway is satisfied when the record addresses human health or health systems, including:

- disease
- illness
- clinical symptoms
- morbidity
- mortality
- injury
- respiratory or cardiovascular health
- human exposure
- health risks
- occupational health
- public health
- healthcare
- health services
- health-system capacity, preparedness, resilience, or functioning

A record qualifies through the health pathway when the climate-related factor/event/agent/fossil fuel is studied in relation to human health or health systems.

Do NOT require a climate-related extreme event if a climate-forcing agent, fossil fuel, or other qualifying climate-related factor is directly related to human health.

For example:
A study measuring atmospheric pollutants and examining respiratory health can qualify through the climate + health pathway when the pollutants include relevant climate-forcing agents.

- Extreme weather events (floods, droughts, storms, storm surges, coastal flooding) -> injuries, fatalities, mental-health effects, health-care disruption;
- Food supply and safety / food security -> undernutrition, foodborne disease;
- Heat stress (heatwaves, cold spells, UV exposure) -> heat-related illness, skin/eye damage;
- Social factors (climate-driven displacement, migration, conflict) -> physical and mental-health effects;

--------------------------------------------------

- reduce greenhouse-gas emissions;
- reduce another climate-forcing emission;
- remove greenhouse gases;
- reduce fossil-fuel use;
- replace fossil fuels;
- reduce dependence on fossil fuels; or
- otherwise mitigate climate change.

An intervention that directly changes or reduces emissions of a climate-forcing agent can qualify as mitigation even when the primary subject of the paper is something else.

A study of dietary sulphur in dairy cattle that examines effects on methane emissions can qualify because:
1. methane is a climate-forcing agent; and
2. an intervention affecting methane emissions constitutes a potential mitigation action.

--------------------------------------------------

- climate adaptation;
- preparedness;
- resilience;
- vulnerability reduction;
- climate-risk management;
- risk reduction;
- adaptation planning;
- preparation for climate-related hazards;
- response to climate-related hazards; or

- future projections;
- climate-risk assessment;
- preparedness;
- resilience planning;
- vulnerability assessment;

- simulations;

--------------------------------------------------

Distinguish between a substantive connection and a merely possible connection.

A. EXPLICIT:
The abstract directly states the climate, health, mitigation, or adaptation relationship.

OR

B. DIRECTLY INFERABLE:

- altered or unusual patterns;
- climate variability;
- climate-related hazards;
- climate impacts;
- mitigation; or
- adaptation.

1. Have no substantive climate-related component.

5. Describe subclinical outcomes that do not manifest as clinical symptoms, unless they are directly relevant to an otherwise qualifying human-health exposure or health risk.

6. Are animal studies with no qualifying climate mitigation, adaptation, human food-security, or human-health connection.

7. Describe an early-stage mitigation/adaptation technology or intervention with no plausible real-world application or deployment.

IMPORTANT:
Do not exclude a record merely because:
- climate change is not the primary topic;
- human health is not the primary topic;
- the study is environmental science, engineering, agriculture, animal science, hydrology, or air pollution research;
- the study is observational;
- the study is computational or modeling-based;
- the study generates experimental data;
- the adaptation action itself has not yet been implemented.

--------------------------------------------------

Example 1:
"Significance of dietary sulphur and sulphate reducing bacteria in lactating dairy cattle"

Decision: INCLUDE

Reason:
The abstract discusses methane gas emissions in relation to an animal-nutrition intervention. Methane is a climate-forcing agent, and an intervention affecting methane emissions can constitute climate mitigation. The primary topic does not need to be climate change or human health.

Example 2:
"Acute effects of air pollution on respiratory health of 50-70 yr old adults"

Decision: INCLUDE

Reason:
The study measures atmospheric pollutants, including relevant climate-forcing pollutants, and directly examines respiratory health. This satisfies the climate + health pathway. A climate-related extreme event, mitigation action, or adaptation action is not additionally required.

Example 3:
"Impact of Tides and Surges on Fluvial Floods in Coastal Regions"

Decision: INCLUDE when the record explicitly connects the modeling to future projections, prevention of flood risks, preparedness, resilience, or adaptation planning.

Reason:
The study addresses a climate-related coastal flooding hazard and produces modeling evidence relevant to future risk management/adaptation. An implemented adaptation intervention is not required.

Example 4:
"Loading and Structural Response of Developed Shorelines Under Waves, Surge, and Tsunami Overland Flow Hazards"

Decision: INCLUDE when the record explicitly connects the research to coastal hazard assessment, risk reduction, resilience, preparedness, or adaptation planning.

Reason:
Experimental or data-generating research can qualify as adaptation-supporting research. The study does not need to implement an adaptation intervention or measure a health outcome.

--------------------------------------------------
10. FINAL DECISION
--------------------------------------------------

Before deciding, ask:

1. What is the substantive climate-related component?
2. Which qualifying pathway applies: health, mitigation, or adaptation?
3. Is that connection explicit or directly inferable from the study?
4. Is the connection substantive rather than merely incidental or hypothetical?

If the answer to question 1 is yes AND at least one qualifying pathway in question 2 is supported by the record, output:

INCLUDE

Otherwise output:

EXCLUDE

Return only the classification:

INCLUDE

or

EXCLUDE

document.name: Complex polymer preparations for the protection of seeds of grain crops of agricultural plants

content.abstract: Pre-sowing treatment of seeds of cultivated plants with agrochemicals can significantly reduce crop losses. A promising technology for increasing the yield of spring crops in arid zones characterized by moisture deficiency in the summer is winter sowing. However, this method carries the risk of large losses as a result of premature germination of grain in the event of prolonged positive temperatures in the fall or severe thaws. Special grain processing chemicals can prevent such losses. Complex polymer preparations have been developed to protect grain seeds from premature germination and damage by phytopathogens. It has been shown that compositions based on polyvinyl acetate dispersions and polyacrylamide most effectively prevent premature germination of barley grains. At the same time, treatment with a copolymer of acrylamide and acrylate significantly reduced plant germination. It has been shown that when barley grains are treated with compositions based on polysaccharides with a fungicidal preparation, fungal infection is completely absent, and there is no significant inhibition of seed germination. This composition for treatment against fungal spoilage of grain and seedlings seems promising for practical use.

- illness
- clinical symptoms

- mortality
- injury
- respiratory or cardiovascular health
- human exposure
- health risks

- healthcare

document.name: Solar Carbothermic Production of Zinc From Zinc Oxide: Solzinc

content.abstract: In late 2004, the pilot Solzinc solar reactor was commissioned. The European Union and the Swiss Federal Office of Science and Education are funding this project to demonstrate the technical feasibility and the economical potential of producing Zn by reducing zinc oxide with the aid of concentrated solar energy and a small amount of carbon at a close to industrial scale. The zinc can be used as a means to store solar energy in a chemical way, e.g. suited to release electricity in Zinc-air fuel cells. This allows on demand use, boosting the availability of solar energy. Furthermore, as the Zinc-air fuel cells’ waste is ZnO, we get a cyclic process by reducing this ZnO in the Solzinc solar reactor. Numerous lab tests and numerical studies of the chemical and thermal behavior of the solar carbothermic ZnO reduction process were conducted by the Swiss Paul Scherrer Institute, the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology, the Israeli Weizmann Institute and the French CNRS Processes, Materials and Solar Energy laboratory. An indirectly heated beam-down reactor concept was chosen and influencing parameters, such as the type of carbon, the stoichiometry of the ZnO-C mix and the process temperature were explored. Based on these findings the technology was scaled up for the pilot plant for about 0.25 MW solar input leading to a designed zinc production rate of 50kg/h. The Swedish company ScanArc Plasma Systems AB developed a special quench system to produce zinc dust directly from the gaseous zinc exhausted from the solar reactor. The dust’s characteristics were adapted to the requirements of the Zn-air fuel cells developed by the German company ZOXY Energy System AG. The resulting zinc can be easily stored and transported for generating electricity as needed. In 2004, the pilot reactor, the quench system and extensive instrumentation were installed at the Weizmann Institute’s solar facilities to process batches of up to 500 kg of ZnO-C mixture. After cold testing of the installation and fulfilling all safety requirements, the first batches were processed. This paper explores the results of the commissioning to show the technical feasibility of this process to produce zinc and to store solar energy.

content.abstract: In the nursing home industry, government regulators are concerned with assuring a high standard of quality, providing the poor with access to care, and controlling the expansion of the industry. To this end, the government has created the Medicaid (and Medicare) patient subsidy programs and the Certificate of Need (CON) cost containment program. This paper theoretically and empirically analyzes the impact of Medicaid and CON policy on nursing home behavior. The theoretical analysis is complicated by the fact that both proprietary and ‘not for profit’ nursing homes exist, and the empirical work is complicated by the problem that quality is not directly observed.

content.abstract: Abstract. It is often difficult to restore the evolution process and energy transfer of ancient landslides that have occurred over a long time. In this paper, the contour restoration method is used to restore the topography before the Mogangling landslide according to the contour of the surrounding mountains. In order to better analyze the landslide movement process and analyze the energy change, the numerical simulation method is used to reproduce the Mogangling landslide. In the process of numerical simulation, the displacement and velocity of the whole and part of the landslide mass are monitored, respectively, so as to extract their potential energy, kinetic energy, and dissipation energy. At the same time, the effective collision of blocks in the process of landslide is obtained by extracting the local peak value of the displacement velocity curve. Meanwhile, the Alpha shape algorithm was employed to extract the volume and surface area of the landslide body from 3D point cloud data, thereby enabling the calculation of its volume expansion rate and area growth rate to quantify the morphological evolution characteristics during the landslide movement process. The results show that for the whole landslide, its energy change conforms to the law of conservation of energy; For some blocks, the energy is not conserved due to the collision and compression of surrounding rock mass; Compared with the upper rock mass, the lower rock mass is compressed more frequently, receives more energy transfer, and has a longer migration distance.
