attribute.prompt:
You are screening bibliographic records for inclusion in the DESTINY repository, a database aimed at capturing the global literature at the intersection of climate change and health, including relevant climate mitigation and adaptation literature.

Your task is to classify each bibliographic record as exactly one of:

INCLUDE
EXCLUDE

Base your decision only on the title, abstract, and other metadata provided. Do not use outside information to fill gaps in the record.

IMPORTANT:
- Do not require climate change, health, mitigation, or adaptation to be the primary topic of the paper.
- Do not require the paper to use the exact words "climate change", "mitigation", or "adaptation".
- Apply the eligibility criteria to each record independently.
- Do not use an assumed prevalence of relevant records to make the decision.
- If the abstract is missing, very short, garbled, or otherwise incomplete, make the best decision possible from the available information.

CORE DECISION RULE

INCLUDE a record if it satisfies:

1. At least one substantive CLIMATE-RELATED component

AND

2. At least one qualifying HEALTH, MITIGATION, or ADAPTATION component.

A record does NOT need to contain a human health outcome if it qualifies through the mitigation or adaptation pathways.

--------------------------------------------------
1. CLIMATE-RELATED COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

A record has a climate-related component if it substantively addresses one or more of the following:

A. Climate change or climate variability

B. Climate/weather variables, such as:
- temperature
- precipitation
- humidity
- wind
- drought
- heat
- cold
- other weather or climate conditions

C. Climate-related extreme events, such as:
- heatwaves
- floods
- droughts
- storms
- hurricanes/cyclones
- storm surges
- wildfires
- other climate-related hazards

D. Fossil fuels or fossil-fuel use, including:
- extraction
- production
- combustion
- consumption
- replacement
- their greenhouse-gas or other climate-forcing emissions (NOT non-climate combustion pollutants such as PAHs or heavy metals — see the air-pollution rule below)

E. Greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents, including:
- methane
- carbon dioxide
- nitrous oxide
- black carbon
- other recognized climate-forcing agents

F. An intervention or action that changes emissions of greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents.

A climate-related component is substantive when the climate-related factor, event, agent, or emission is:
- measured;
- analyzed;
- modeled;
- used as an exposure;
- used as an outcome;
- affected by an intervention; or
- otherwise important to the research question.

The climate-related component does NOT need to be the main topic of the paper.

For example:
- An animal nutrition study that evaluates methane emissions can have a climate-related component because methane is a climate-forcing agent.
- An air-pollution study can have a climate-related component when it studies a recognized climate-forcing pollutant/agent.
- A flood model can have a climate-related component when it studies a climate-related flood hazard.

DO NOT consider a record climate-related merely because climate change, temperature, fossil fuels, greenhouse gases, or another climate-related term appears incidentally in the background, introduction, discussion, or references.

IMPORTANT:
Air pollution in general is NOT automatically a climate-related component. The climate criterion is satisfied only when the pollutant is itself a relevant climate-forcing agent or the record explicitly connects the pollution to climate change.

IMPORTANT — INTENT:
A greenhouse gas, climate-forcing agent, or fossil-fuel substance makes a record climate-related ONLY when the study concerns it as a climate, energy, emissions, or air-quality matter. It does NOT qualify when the substance is present for an unrelated reason, e.g.: a greenhouse gas studied as a drug or toxicant (recreational nitrous-oxide abuse); a single fossil-fuel-derived chemical studied only for cellular/clinical toxicology (a diesel-exhaust compound tested in vitro); fossil-fuel infrastructure studied only as an industrial-accident or safety hazard (a pipeline explosion). The agent must be substantive to the research question as a climate/energy/emissions matter, not merely named.

--------------------------------------------------
2. QUALIFYING HEALTH COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The health pathway is satisfied when the record addresses human health or health systems, including:

- disease
- illness
- clinical symptoms
- morbidity
- mortality
- injury
- respiratory or cardiovascular health
- human exposure
- health risks
- occupational health
- public health
- healthcare
- health services
- health-system capacity, preparedness, resilience, or functioning

A record qualifies through the health pathway when the climate-related factor/event/agent/fossil fuel is studied in relation to human health or health systems.

Do NOT require a climate-related extreme event if a climate-forcing agent, fossil fuel, or other qualifying climate-related factor is directly related to human health.

For example:
A study measuring atmospheric pollutants and examining respiratory health can qualify through the climate + health pathway when the pollutants include relevant climate-forcing agents.

Do NOT infer human-health relevance merely because an environmental condition, pollutant, animal disease, agricultural outcome, or ecosystem change could theoretically affect human health.

INDIRECT HEALTH VIA CLIMATE EXPOSURE PATHWAYS (CCHE):
The health component is ALSO satisfied when the record substantively addresses a recognised climate-health exposure pathway through which climate/weather or a climate-forcing agent affects human health, even without a named clinical outcome. The recognised pathways are:
- Air quality (particulate matter, ground-level ozone, wildfire smoke/haze, pollen/aeroallergens, dust storms) -> respiratory/cardiovascular disease;
- Extreme weather events (floods, droughts, storms, storm surges, coastal flooding) -> injuries, fatalities, mental-health effects, health-care disruption;
- Food supply and safety / food security -> undernutrition, foodborne disease;
- Heat stress (heatwaves, cold spells, UV exposure) -> heat-related illness, skin/eye damage;
- Social factors (climate-driven displacement, migration, conflict) -> physical and mental-health effects;
- Vector distribution and ecology (mosquitoes, ticks, rodents, sandflies) -> vector-borne disease (malaria, dengue, Lyme, West Nile, etc.);
- Water quality and quantity (waterborne pathogens, HARMFUL ALGAL BLOOMS / cyanobacteria, drought- or flood-related contamination) -> cholera, cryptosporidiosis, diarrhoeal disease, etc.
A study of one of these exposures in a climate/weather or fossil-fuel/climate-forcing-agent context satisfies the health component through the indirect pathway. This does NOT override the guard above: a merely hypothetical or unstated health link still does not qualify -- the exposure pathway must be a substantive subject of the record.

--------------------------------------------------
3. QUALIFYING MITIGATION COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The mitigation pathway is satisfied when the record studies an action, intervention, technology, practice, policy, or management strategy that is intended to:

- reduce greenhouse-gas emissions;
- reduce another climate-forcing emission;
- remove greenhouse gases;
- reduce fossil-fuel use;
- replace fossil fuels;
- reduce dependence on fossil fuels; or
- otherwise mitigate climate change.

The record does not need to use the word "mitigation".

An intervention that directly changes or reduces emissions of a climate-forcing agent can qualify as mitigation even when the primary subject of the paper is something else.

For example:
A study of dietary sulphur in dairy cattle that examines effects on methane emissions can qualify because:
1. methane is a climate-forcing agent; and
2. an intervention affecting methane emissions constitutes a potential mitigation action.

Merely measuring methane, carbon dioxide, or another greenhouse gas does NOT by itself constitute mitigation.

The record must study an intervention, action, practice, technology, policy, or management approach that affects or is intended to affect emissions or fossil-fuel use.

IMPORTANT — A MITIGATION ACTION, NOT ENABLING RESEARCH:
The record must study, evaluate, or report the mitigation action itself — an intervention, measure, practice, policy, deployment, or management approach that reduces, or is intended to reduce, emissions or fossil-fuel use, or that upscales greenhouse-gas removals. Upstream, basic, or enabling research that merely relates to, characterises, or could inform a low-carbon technology — without itself studying an emission-reducing action or its effect on emissions or fossil-fuel use — does NOT qualify. For example: soil-physics, materials, or component modelling that "supports the design of" a geothermal or other renewable-energy system is enabling research, not a mitigation action; whereas evaluating a feed intervention that reduces methane emissions, or measures that cut a product's manufacturing emissions, IS a mitigation action.

--------------------------------------------------
4. QUALIFYING ADAPTATION COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The adaptation pathway is satisfied when the record addresses:

- climate adaptation;
- preparedness;
- resilience;
- vulnerability reduction;
- climate-risk management;
- risk reduction;
- adaptation planning;
- preparation for climate-related hazards;
- response to climate-related hazards; or
- assessment of future climate-related risks for decision-making.

Adaptation does not have to mean an intervention that has already been implemented.

Research can qualify as adaptation-supporting research when it directly generates evidence needed for:
- adaptation planning;
- future projections;
- climate-risk assessment;
- preparedness;
- resilience planning;
- vulnerability assessment;
- hazard management; or
- risk reduction.

This includes relevant:
- models;
- datasets;
- experiments;
- projections;
- simulations;
- risk assessments;
- engineering studies;
- monitoring studies;
- decision-support tools.

For example:
A study modeling storm surges and compound coastal flooding can qualify if the study explicitly connects the results to future projections, prevention of flood risks, preparedness, resilience, or adaptation planning.

A study generating experimental data on storm surge, wave, or tsunami impacts on coastal structures can qualify when the research is directly relevant to assessment of coastal hazards, resilience, risk reduction, or adaptation planning.

IMPORTANT:
The exclusion for early-stage research applies primarily to immature mitigation/adaptation TECHNOLOGIES or INTERVENTIONS that are not ready for plausible real-world use.

Do NOT exclude ordinary scientific research, modeling, experiments, or data-generation merely because they are not themselves an implemented adaptation action.

IMPORTANT — ADAPTATION PURPOSE:
The adaptation pathway requires the record to frame its purpose, explicitly or by direct inference, as informing human or societal climate adaptation, preparedness, resilience, or climate-risk management. The following do NOT qualify on their own: physiological/biological acclimation of organisms to temperature (the organism adapting is not climate-adaptation research); routine drainage, civil-engineering, or infrastructure studies with no stated climate-risk or adaptation purpose; descriptions of an ecosystem's protective function without a stated adaptation, risk-reduction, or resilience purpose. "Resilience", "vulnerability", or "adaptation" used in a biological or generic-engineering sense does not satisfy this pathway.

IMPORTANT -- ADAPTATION MUST PROTECT HUMAN HEALTH, HEALTH SYSTEMS, OR HUMAN-IMPORTANT ECOSYSTEMS:
The adaptation pathway is satisfied ONLY when the action or supporting research is intended to reduce the exposure or vulnerability of human health, health systems, or ecosystems of importance to humans (e.g. pollinators, protective or food-producing ecosystems) to actual or expected climate hazards -- typically a hazard that acts on humans through one of the recognised climate-health exposure pathways (air quality, extreme weather, food security, heat, social factors, vectors, water). Adaptation or resilience of purely physical, industrial, or economic assets with no human-health, health-system, or human-important-ecosystem target does NOT qualify. For example: protecting or optimising energy systems or industrial infrastructure against climate variability, or protecting land/soil from erosion, is out of scope unless the record connects it to human health, health systems, or a human-important ecosystem. Protecting human settlements or populations from coastal flooding, storm surge, or other extreme-weather hazards DOES qualify (extreme-weather exposure pathway).

--------------------------------------------------

--------------------------------------------------

Distinguish between a substantive connection and a merely possible connection.

INCLUDE when the qualifying connection is:

A. EXPLICIT:
The abstract directly states the climate, health, mitigation, or adaptation relationship.

OR

B. DIRECTLY INFERABLE:
The relationship follows directly from what the study measures, evaluates, models, or changes.

For example:
- An intervention changes methane emissions -> mitigation is directly inferable.
- A climate-forcing pollutant is associated with respiratory symptoms -> climate + health is directly inferable.
- A coastal flood model is explicitly intended to inform future risk prevention -> adaptation relevance is explicit.

For example:
- A generic environmental study that could potentially be useful for climate adaptation but does not indicate any adaptation, climate-risk, future-projection, resilience, or preparedness purpose.
- A pollutant study where the pollutant is not a climate-forcing agent and no climate connection is stated.
- A study of animal health where a human-health implication is merely possible.

Animal health alone is not equivalent to human health.

- climate variability;
- climate-related hazards;

Do not exclude a record merely because it contains seasonal data if the study also addresses a qualifying climate-related question.

document.name: Chemical composition and nutritional properties of Terminalia catappa L. oil and kernels from Benin

content.abstract: This work focuses on the physico-chemical characterization of kernels and oil of Terminalia catappa L. from Benin. The detailed physico-chemical properties are given including the nutritional composition and fatty acid profile, but also the phenolic content, phytochemical screening and antioxidant capacity which were determined for the first time. The kernel (100 g) contained 5.5 g of moisture, a high level of lipids (64.7–140.4 of Recommended Daily Intake (RDI)), proteins (36.0% RDI), sugars (6.0% RDI), and tannins (0.6%). The defatted kernels (100 g) contained high levels of manganese (184.8–236.1% RDI), magnesium (173.6–235.2% RDI), iron (89.7–201.9% RDI), zinc (87.9–120.9% RDI) and calcium (41.5% RDI), and contributed for 98.6% of RDI proteins. The kernel oil showed a high level of unsaturated fatty acids including oleic (27.1%) and linoleic acids (26.6%) and saturated fatty acids such as palmitic acid (40.0%) as well as several phytosterols and triterpenes. These kernels and their unsaturated oil are of interesting nutritional value but could also be used as a biofuel or lubricant. The presence of phenolic and terpenic derivatives may also explain at least in part their use in traditional medicine.

document.name: Application of GIS for Risk Identification and Assessment of the Road Infrastructure from the Occurrence of Landslide Processes - Study for the Territory of Sliven Region, Bulgaria

content.abstract: The paper is focused on using the capabilities of GIS in order to determine how appropriate their application is for identification and assessment of the risk to the road infrastructure from the occurrence of landslide processes. Based on the available data for landslides and other free and open-source resources, numerous spatial analyses have been performed on different layers and parameters have been derived to determine the most vulnerable sections of the road infrastructure on the territory of Sliven region. The results are classified and described in relation to the road network for the territory, and a comparison is made with the data from the risk map published with the Landslide Register. In the validation of the results, it is found that in some areas there is a higher level of compliance with the risk map, but in others there are differences, which have been further analyzed, and it is found that these are mainly the areas where landslide processes have already been registered, as well as other places that meet the same criteria.

document.name: Analytical model of fully developed wind farms in conventionally neutral atmospheric boundary layers

content.abstract: The wind energy industry relies on computationally efficient engineering-type models to design wind farms. Typically these models do not account for the effect of atmospheric stratification in either the boundary layer or the free atmosphere. This study proposes a new analytical model for fully developed wind-turbine arrays in conventionally neutral atmospheric boundary layers frequently encountered in nature. The model captures the effect of the free-atmosphere stratification, Coriolis force, wind farm layout and turbine operating condition on the wind farm performance. The model is developed based on the physical insight derived from large-eddy simulations. We demonstrate that the geostrophic drag law (GDL) for flow over flat terrain can be extended to flow over fully developed wind farm arrays. The presence of a vast wind farm significantly increases the wind farm friction velocity compared with flow over flat terrain, which is modelled by updated coefficients in the GDL. The developed model reliably captures the vertical wind speed profile inside the wind farm. Furthermore, the power production trends observed in simulations are reliably reproduced. The wind farm performance, normalized by the geostrophic wind speed, decreases as the free-atmosphere thermal stability increases or the Coriolis force decreases. In addition, we find that the optimal wind farm performance is obtained at a lower thrust coefficient than the Betz limit, which indicates that optimal operating conditions for turbines in a wind farm are different than for a single turbine.

document.name: Overexpression of spinach non-symbiotic hemoglobin in Arabidopsis resulted in decreased NO content and lowered nitrate and other abiotic stresses tolerance

content.abstract: A class 1 non-symbiotic hemoglobin family gene, SoHb, was isolated from spinach. qRT-PCR showed that SoHb was induced by excess nitrate, polyethylene glycol, NaCl, H2O2, and salicylic acid. Besides, SoHb was strongly induced by application of nitric oxide (NO) donor, while was suppressed by NO scavenger, nitrate reductase inhibitor, and nitric oxide synthase inhibitor. Overexpression of SoHb in Arabidopsis resulted in decreased NO level and sensitivity to nitrate stress, as shown by reduced root length, fresh weight, the maximum photosystem II quantum ratio of variable to maximum fluorescence (Fv/Fm), and higher malondialdehyde contents. The activities and gene transcription of superoxide dioxidase, and catalase decreased under nitrate stress. Expression levels of RD22, RD29A, DREB2A, and P5CS1 decreased after nitrate treatment in SoHb-overexpressing plants, while increased in the WT plants. Moreover, SoHb-overexpressing plants showed decreased tolerance to NaCl and osmotic stress. In addition, the SoHb-overexpression lines showed earlier flower by regulating the expression of SOC, GI and FLC genes. Our results indicated that the decreasing NO content in Arabidopsis by overexpressing SoHb might be responsible for lowered tolerance to nitrate and other abiotic stresses.

document.name: The Connotation Value, Design and Implementation of Outdoor Games for Infants under the Concept of Natural Education

content.abstract: 当前社会城市化快速发展，婴幼儿的成长环境与自然逐渐疏远。基于自然教育理念，户外游戏对婴幼儿的身体健康成长、认知学习能力、情绪和社会性发展具有重要意义。文章探索出确定自然节律游戏主题、开拓机构内外的户外游戏场地、选择自然环保的游戏材料、创新户外游戏玩法的设计构想；结合实践案例，提出创设生动有趣的户外游戏情境、充分释放婴幼儿游戏的自主权、注重多种形式的游戏奖励的实践策略。With the rapid development of urbanization, the growth environment of infants and young children is gradually alienated from nature. Based on the concept of natural education, outdoor games are of great significance to the healthy growth, cognitive learning ability, emotional and social development of infants and young children. This paper explores the design ideas of determining the theme of natural rhythm game, developing outdoor game venues inside and outside the organization, selecting natural and environmentally friendly game materials, and innovating outdoor game play. Based on practical cases, this paper proposes practical strategies such as creating vivid and interesting outdoor game scenarios, fully releasing the autonomy of infants and toddlers in games, and emphasizing various forms of game rewards.

attribute.prompt:
You are screening bibliographic records for inclusion in the DESTINY repository, a database aimed at capturing the global literature at the intersection of climate change and health, including relevant climate mitigation and adaptation literature.

Your task is to classify each bibliographic record as exactly one of:

INCLUDE
EXCLUDE

Base your decision only on the title, abstract, and other metadata provided. Do not use outside information to fill gaps in the record.

IMPORTANT:
- Do not require climate change, health, mitigation, or adaptation to be the primary topic of the paper.
- Do not require the paper to use the exact words "climate change", "mitigation", or "adaptation".

- Do not use an assumed prevalence of relevant records to make the decision.
- If the abstract is missing, very short, garbled, or otherwise incomplete, make the best decision possible from the available information.

CORE DECISION RULE

INCLUDE a record if it satisfies:

1. At least one substantive CLIMATE-RELATED component

AND

2. At least one qualifying HEALTH, MITIGATION, or ADAPTATION component.

A record does NOT need to contain a human health outcome if it qualifies through the mitigation or adaptation pathways.

--------------------------------------------------
1. CLIMATE-RELATED COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

A record has a climate-related component if it substantively addresses one or more of the following:

A. Climate change or climate variability

B. Climate/weather variables, such as:
- temperature
- precipitation
- humidity
- wind
- drought
- heat
- cold
- other weather or climate conditions

C. Climate-related extreme events, such as:
- heatwaves
- floods
- droughts
- storms
- hurricanes/cyclones
- storm surges
- wildfires
- other climate-related hazards

D. Fossil fuels or fossil-fuel use, including:
- extraction
- production
- combustion
- consumption
- replacement
- their greenhouse-gas or other climate-forcing emissions (NOT non-climate combustion pollutants such as PAHs or heavy metals — see the air-pollution rule below)

E. Greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents, including:
- methane
- carbon dioxide
- nitrous oxide
- black carbon
- other recognized climate-forcing agents

F. An intervention or action that changes emissions of greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents.

A climate-related component is substantive when the climate-related factor, event, agent, or emission is:
- measured;
- analyzed;
- modeled;
- used as an exposure;
- used as an outcome;
- affected by an intervention; or
- otherwise important to the research question.

The climate-related component does NOT need to be the main topic of the paper.

For example:
- An animal nutrition study that evaluates methane emissions can have a climate-related component because methane is a climate-forcing agent.
- An air-pollution study can have a climate-related component when it studies a recognized climate-forcing pollutant/agent.
- A flood model can have a climate-related component when it studies a climate-related flood hazard.

DO NOT consider a record climate-related merely because climate change, temperature, fossil fuels, greenhouse gases, or another climate-related term appears incidentally in the background, introduction, discussion, or references.

IMPORTANT:
Air pollution in general is NOT automatically a climate-related component. The climate criterion is satisfied only when the pollutant is itself a relevant climate-forcing agent or the record explicitly connects the pollution to climate change.

IMPORTANT — INTENT:
A greenhouse gas, climate-forcing agent, or fossil-fuel substance makes a record climate-related ONLY when the study concerns it as a climate, energy, emissions, or air-quality matter. It does NOT qualify when the substance is present for an unrelated reason, e.g.: a greenhouse gas studied as a drug or toxicant (recreational nitrous-oxide abuse); a single fossil-fuel-derived chemical studied only for cellular/clinical toxicology (a diesel-exhaust compound tested in vitro); fossil-fuel infrastructure studied only as an industrial-accident or safety hazard (a pipeline explosion). The agent must be substantive to the research question as a climate/energy/emissions matter, not merely named.

--------------------------------------------------
2. QUALIFYING HEALTH COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The health pathway is satisfied when the record addresses human health or health systems, including:

- disease
- illness
- clinical symptoms
- morbidity
- mortality
- injury
- respiratory or cardiovascular health
- human exposure
- health risks
- occupational health
- public health
- healthcare
- health services
- health-system capacity, preparedness, resilience, or functioning

A record qualifies through the health pathway when the climate-related factor/event/agent/fossil fuel is studied in relation to human health or health systems.

Do NOT require a climate-related extreme event if a climate-forcing agent, fossil fuel, or other qualifying climate-related factor is directly related to human health.

For example:
A study measuring atmospheric pollutants and examining respiratory health can qualify through the climate + health pathway when the pollutants include relevant climate-forcing agents.

Do NOT infer human-health relevance merely because an environmental condition, pollutant, animal disease, agricultural outcome, or ecosystem change could theoretically affect human health.

INDIRECT HEALTH VIA CLIMATE EXPOSURE PATHWAYS (CCHE):
The health component is ALSO satisfied when the record substantively addresses a recognised climate-health exposure pathway through which climate/weather or a climate-forcing agent affects human health, even without a named clinical outcome. The recognised pathways are:
- Air quality (particulate matter, ground-level ozone, wildfire smoke/haze, pollen/aeroallergens, dust storms) -> respiratory/cardiovascular disease;
- Extreme weather events (floods, droughts, storms, storm surges, coastal flooding) -> injuries, fatalities, mental-health effects, health-care disruption;
- Food supply and safety / food security -> undernutrition, foodborne disease;
- Heat stress (heatwaves, cold spells, UV exposure) -> heat-related illness, skin/eye damage;
- Social factors (climate-driven displacement, migration, conflict) -> physical and mental-health effects;
- Vector distribution and ecology (mosquitoes, ticks, rodents, sandflies) -> vector-borne disease (malaria, dengue, Lyme, West Nile, etc.);
- Water quality and quantity (waterborne pathogens, HARMFUL ALGAL BLOOMS / cyanobacteria, drought- or flood-related contamination) -> cholera, cryptosporidiosis, diarrhoeal disease, etc.
A study of one of these exposures in a climate/weather or fossil-fuel/climate-forcing-agent context satisfies the health component through the indirect pathway. This does NOT override the guard above: a merely hypothetical or unstated health link still does not qualify -- the exposure pathway must be a substantive subject of the record.

--------------------------------------------------
3. QUALIFYING MITIGATION COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The mitigation pathway is satisfied when the record studies an action, intervention, technology, practice, policy, or management strategy that is intended to:

- reduce greenhouse-gas emissions;
- reduce another climate-forcing emission;
- remove greenhouse gases;
- reduce fossil-fuel use;
- replace fossil fuels;
- reduce dependence on fossil fuels; or
- otherwise mitigate climate change.

An intervention that directly changes or reduces emissions of a climate-forcing agent can qualify as mitigation even when the primary subject of the paper is something else.

For example:
A study of dietary sulphur in dairy cattle that examines effects on methane emissions can qualify because:
1. methane is a climate-forcing agent; and
2. an intervention affecting methane emissions constitutes a potential mitigation action.

Merely measuring methane, carbon dioxide, or another greenhouse gas does NOT by itself constitute mitigation.

The record must study an intervention, action, practice, technology, policy, or management approach that affects or is intended to affect emissions or fossil-fuel use.

IMPORTANT — A MITIGATION ACTION, NOT ENABLING RESEARCH:
The record must study, evaluate, or report the mitigation action itself — an intervention, measure, practice, policy, deployment, or management approach that reduces, or is intended to reduce, emissions or fossil-fuel use, or that upscales greenhouse-gas removals. Upstream, basic, or enabling research that merely relates to, characterises, or could inform a low-carbon technology — without itself studying an emission-reducing action or its effect on emissions or fossil-fuel use — does NOT qualify. For example: soil-physics, materials, or component modelling that "supports the design of" a geothermal or other renewable-energy system is enabling research, not a mitigation action; whereas evaluating a feed intervention that reduces methane emissions, or measures that cut a product's manufacturing emissions, IS a mitigation action.

--------------------------------------------------
4. QUALIFYING ADAPTATION COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The adaptation pathway is satisfied when the record addresses:

- climate adaptation;
- preparedness;
- resilience;
- vulnerability reduction;
- climate-risk management;
- risk reduction;
- adaptation planning;
- preparation for climate-related hazards;
- response to climate-related hazards; or
- assessment of future climate-related risks for decision-making.

Adaptation does not have to mean an intervention that has already been implemented.

Research can qualify as adaptation-supporting research when it directly generates evidence needed for:
- adaptation planning;
- future projections;
- climate-risk assessment;
- preparedness;
- resilience planning;
- vulnerability assessment;
- hazard management; or
- risk reduction.

This includes relevant:
- models;
- datasets;
- experiments;
- projections;
- simulations;
- risk assessments;
- engineering studies;
- monitoring studies;
- decision-support tools.

For example:
A study modeling storm surges and compound coastal flooding can qualify if the study explicitly connects the results to future projections, prevention of flood risks, preparedness, resilience, or adaptation planning.

A study generating experimental data on storm surge, wave, or tsunami impacts on coastal structures can qualify when the research is directly relevant to assessment of coastal hazards, resilience, risk reduction, or adaptation planning.

The exclusion for early-stage research applies primarily to immature mitigation/adaptation TECHNOLOGIES or INTERVENTIONS that are not ready for plausible real-world use.

Do NOT exclude ordinary scientific research, modeling, experiments, or data-generation merely because they are not themselves an implemented adaptation action.

The adaptation pathway requires the record to frame its purpose, explicitly or by direct inference, as informing human or societal climate adaptation, preparedness, resilience, or climate-risk management. The following do NOT qualify on their own: physiological/biological acclimation of organisms to temperature (the organism adapting is not climate-adaptation research); routine drainage, civil-engineering, or infrastructure studies with no stated climate-risk or adaptation purpose; descriptions of an ecosystem's protective function without a stated adaptation, risk-reduction, or resilience purpose. Protecting human settlements or populations from coastal flooding, storm surge, or other extreme-weather hazards DOES qualify (extreme-weather exposure pathway).

--------------------------------------------------

Distinguish between a substantive connection and a merely possible connection.

A. EXPLICIT:
The abstract directly states the climate, health, mitigation, or adaptation relationship.

OR

The relationship follows directly from what the study measures, evaluates, models, or changes.

content.abstract: Molecular identification is a fundamental issue in astrobiology to investigate the routes of emergence of life on our planet involving in particular a potential seeding of extraterrestrial organic matter on the primitive Earth. However, this project encompasses major difficulties due to the low concentration of molecules present in bodies of the Solar System. This work proposes an integrative analytical workflow, no longer based on GC-MS instruments, to enhance comprehensive analysis of organic markers in these objects. Our strategy combines UPLC-HRMS and UPLC-MRM MS methods to bring both a broad molecular mapping and detailed data on indigenous compounds present in any extraterrestrial objects or laboratory analogs. Applied on water extracts from fresh meteorites, our workflow highlights a wide range of free molecules in the non-treated extracts and reveals the wide diversity of amino acid and nucleobase isomers that could lead to misinterpretation as far as the molecular composition of meteorite extracts cannot be anticipated. This strategy, never explored so far, would provide new clues for studying the organic matter in space and should offer new perspectives on its evolution and reactivity.

document.name: Regime Interaction and Climate Change

content.abstract: The regulation of greenhouse gas emissions from international aviation and maritime transport has proved to be a difficult task for international climate negotiations such as the Paris Agreement in 2015. Almost two decades prior, Article 2.2 of the Kyoto Protocol excluded emissions from international aviation and maritime transport from its targets, delegating the negotiation of sector-specific regulations to the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and the International Maritime Organization (IMO), respectively. However, progress at these venues has also been limited. Regime Interaction and Climate Change maps out the legal frameworks in the Climate, ICAO and IMO regimes, and explores the law-making process for the regulation of international aviation and maritime transport through the lenses of fragmentation of international law and regime interaction. The book sheds light on how interaction between these three regimes occurs, what the consequences of such interaction are and how they can be managed to resolve conflicts and promote synergies. This book will be of great interest to scholars of international environmental law and governance, climate change policy and climate change law.

- adaptation.

- the study is computational or modeling-based;
- the study generates experimental data;
- the adaptation action itself has not yet been implemented.

The abstract discusses methane gas emissions in relation to an animal-nutrition intervention. Methane is a climate-forcing agent, and an intervention affecting methane emissions can constitute climate mitigation. The primary topic does not need to be climate change or human health.

Decision: INCLUDE

Reason:

Reason:

Decision: INCLUDE when the record explicitly connects the research to coastal hazard assessment, risk reduction, resilience, preparedness, or adaptation planning.

Reason:
Experimental or data-generating research can qualify as adaptation-supporting research. The study does not need to implement an adaptation intervention or measure a health outcome.

1. What is the substantive climate-related component?
2. Which qualifying pathway applies: health, mitigation, or adaptation?
3. Is that connection explicit or directly inferable from the study?
4. Is the connection substantive rather than merely incidental or hypothetical?

If the answer to question 1 is yes AND at least one qualifying pathway in question 2 is supported by the record, output:

INCLUDE

Otherwise output:

EXCLUDE

Return only the classification:

INCLUDE

or

EXCLUDE

document.name: Youth and Political Violence in India: A Social Psychological Account of Conflict Experiences from the Kashmir Valley

content.abstract: "This book offers a socio-cultural and interdisciplinary understanding of the impact of political violence on youth behaviour. Drawing on extensive fieldwork in the Kashmir Valley and reports from conflict areas across the globe, the volume brings to focus the ways in which violence affects social and psychological dynamics within the individual and the community. It develops a social-psychological approach to the study of youth and violent conflict in South Asia and offers new insights into the intricacies within the discourse, Focussing on the emotions and behaviour of people in large-scale conflict, it expands the discourse on the psychological dimensions of hope, aggression, emotion regulation the extremist mindset and policy and intervention for peace building. Moving beyond western psychiatric models, this book proposes a more culturally and historically rooted analysis that focuses on collective experiences of violence to de-colonise psychological science and expand the understanding of youth's experiences with political violence. The volume will be of great interest to scholars and researchers of politics, psychology, peace and conflict studies, sociology and social anthropology"--

document.name: Effect of the β-glucan from Lentinus edodes on colitis-associated colorectal cancer and gut microbiota

content.abstract: Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer in the world, and therapies with safety are in great need. In this study, the β-glucan isolated from Lentinus edodes was successfully fractionated into three fractions with different weight-average molecular weight (M<sub>w</sub>) by ultrasonic degradation and used for the treatment of colorectal cancer. In our findings, the β-glucan was successfully degraded with the M<sub>w</sub> decreased from 2.56 × 10<sup>6</sup> Da to 1.41 × 10<sup>6</sup> Da, exhibiting the triple helix structure without conformation disruption. The in vitro results indicate that β-glucan fractions inhibited colon cancer cell proliferation, induced colon cancer cell apoptosis, and reduced inflammation. The in vivo results based on Azoxymethane (AOM)/dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) mouse model demonstrate that the lower-molecular weight β-glucan fraction showed stronger anti-inflammatory and anti-colon cancer activities by reconstructing intestinal mucosal barrier, increasing short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) content, regulating metabolism of gut microbiota, and rebuilding the gut microbiota structure with the increased Bacteroides and the decreased Proteobacteria at the phylum level, as well as with the decreased Helicobacter and the increased Muribaculum at the genus level. These findings provide scientific basis for using the β-glucan to regulate gut microbiota as an alternative strategy in the clinical treatment of colon cancer.

1. At least one substantive CLIMATE-RELATED component

A record does NOT need to contain a human health outcome if it qualifies through the mitigation or adaptation pathways.

--------------------------------------------------
1. CLIMATE-RELATED COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

A record has a climate-related component if it substantively addresses one or more of the following:

A. Climate change or climate variability

B. Climate/weather variables, such as:
- temperature
- precipitation
- humidity
- wind
- drought
- heat
- cold
- other weather or climate conditions

C. Climate-related extreme events, such as:
- heatwaves
- floods
- droughts
- storms
- hurricanes/cyclones
- storm surges
- wildfires
- other climate-related hazards

D. Fossil fuels or fossil-fuel use, including:
- extraction
- production
- combustion
- consumption
- replacement
- their greenhouse-gas or other climate-forcing emissions (NOT non-climate combustion pollutants such as PAHs or heavy metals — see the air-pollution rule below)

- methane
- carbon dioxide
- nitrous oxide
- black carbon
- other recognized climate-forcing agents

- measured;
- analyzed;
- modeled;
- used as an exposure;
- used as an outcome;
- affected by an intervention; or
- otherwise important to the research question.

The agent must be substantive to the research question as a climate/energy/emissions matter, not merely named.

--------------------------------------------------
2. QUALIFYING HEALTH COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The health pathway is satisfied when the record addresses human health or health systems, including:

- disease
- illness
- clinical symptoms
- morbidity
- mortality
- injury
- respiratory or cardiovascular health
- human exposure
- health risks
- occupational health
- public health
- healthcare
- health services
- health-system capacity, preparedness, resilience, or functioning

A record qualifies through the health pathway when the climate-related factor/event/agent/fossil fuel is studied in relation to human health or health systems.

Do NOT require a climate-related extreme event if a climate-forcing agent, fossil fuel, or other qualifying climate-related factor is directly related to human health.

For example:
A study measuring atmospheric pollutants and examining respiratory health can qualify through the climate + health pathway when the pollutants include relevant climate-forcing agents.

Do NOT infer human-health relevance merely because an environmental condition, pollutant, animal disease, agricultural outcome, or ecosystem change could theoretically affect human health.

- Extreme weather events (floods, droughts, storms, storm surges, coastal flooding) -> injuries, fatalities, mental-health effects, health-care disruption;
- Food supply and safety / food security -> undernutrition, foodborne disease;
- Heat stress (heatwaves, cold spells, UV exposure) -> heat-related illness, skin/eye damage;
- Social factors (climate-driven displacement, migration, conflict) -> physical and mental-health effects;
- Vector distribution and ecology (mosquitoes, ticks, rodents, sandflies) -> vector-borne disease (malaria, dengue, Lyme, West Nile, etc.);

--------------------------------------------------

- reduce fossil-fuel use;

--------------------------------------------------

The adaptation pathway is satisfied when the record addresses:

- preparedness;
- resilience;
- vulnerability reduction;
- climate-risk management;
- risk reduction;
- adaptation planning;
- preparation for climate-related hazards;
- response to climate-related hazards; or
- assessment of future climate-related risks for decision-making.

- future projections;
- climate-risk assessment;
- preparedness;
- resilience planning;
- vulnerability assessment;
- hazard management; or
- risk reduction.

This includes relevant:
- models;
- datasets;
- experiments;
- projections;
- simulations;
- risk assessments;
- engineering studies;
- monitoring studies;
- decision-support tools.

For example:

The adaptation pathway requires the record to frame its purpose, explicitly or by direct inference, as informing human or societal climate adaptation, preparedness, resilience, or climate-risk management. The following do NOT qualify on their own: physiological/biological acclimation of organisms to temperature (the organism adapting is not climate-adaptation research); routine drainage, civil-engineering, or infrastructure studies with no stated climate-risk or adaptation purpose; descriptions of an ecosystem's protective function without a stated adaptation, risk-reduction, or resilience purpose. document.name: Preharvest Application of Seaweed Based Biostimulant Reduced Cherry (Prunus Avium L.) Cracking

content.abstract: Nowadays, consumers are increasingly demanding in relation to cherry, expecting fruits with good size, firmness and flavour, while the producer aims to achieve higher and regular yields, searching to reduce fruit losses, mainly caused by fruit cracking, which is related to several factors, including genotype, soil type and volume and intensity of rainfall (1-4). The climate change predictions point to an increase in the duration of excess rainfall before harvest that may cause higher cherry cracking. Several strategies to reduce this physiological disorder are described, mainly the application of minerals or other chemicals, that delay or reduces the water uptake to fruit, increase the transpiration of free water from the fruit surface or improve the fruit skin properties (5-7). Therefore, this work aimed to study the effect of a biostimulant application in production, size, cracking index, cracking size, fruit waxes content, pH, titratable acidity, soluble solids and nutritional characteristics of the fruits from two cherry cultivars, Sweetheart and Skeena, grafted on Gisela 6. This study was carried out in an orchard installed in Carrazedo de Montenegro, northeast of Portugal. The treatment consisted in the application of a biostimulant composed mainly of seaweed extract (Ascophyllum nodosum) in three applications during 2014. For both cultivars, the application of the biostimulant promoted a significant reduction (p<0.05) of cracking index and a significant increase (p<0.05) of weight, width, diameter, pH and fruit waxes content. Furthermore, negative correlations were found between cracking size and fruit dimensions (weight, r=-0.575 and diameter, r=-0.517; p<0.05). Regarding nutritional characteristics, the quality of the fruits was unaffected by the treatment with biostimulant, while yield remained constant. This study showed that the application of biostimulant reduced the production losses caused by cracking without compromising either the quality or the yield in the studied cultivars.

document.name: Youth theatre and the climate crisis in Australia: the role of ‘unmediatised liveness’ in performing recovery, resistance, and survival

content.abstract: This paper presents the provocation that ‘unmediatised liveness', or experiences not filtered through digital technology, is vital to performances that promote recovery, resistance, and survival among young people in response to the climate crisis. Our provocation draws from interviews conducted with youth theatre and performance practitioners in Australia whose work addresses the climate crisis holistically across disaster preparedness, first response, disaster recovery, and climate activism. We argue that while mediatised interactions remain a critical element of contemporary youth culture and performance, unmediatised co-presence, artistic collaboration, community action, and activism are crucial in the high-stakes context of Australia’s climate crisis.

document.name: REVERSAL OF INSULIN RESISTANCE IN DIABETIC RAT ADIPOCYTES BY INSULIN THERAPY - RESTORATION OF POOL OF GLUCOSE TRANSPORTERS AND ENHANCEMENT OF GLUCOSE-TRANSPORT ACTIVITY

content.abstract: To determine the role of insulin in reversing the insulin resistance associated with depletion of the intracellular pool of glucose transporters, streptozocin-induced diabetic rats were treated with 5 U/day s.c. of insulin for 0, 8, or 14 days. At each time point, adipose cells were isolated, and 3-O-methylglucose transport was measured in the absence and presence of 1000 .mu.U/ml insulin. With the cytochalasin B-binding assay, concentrations of glucose transporters in the plasma and the low-density microsomal membrane fractions were determined. Eight-day insulin therapy enhanced glucose transport rate (mean .+-. SE) from 0.2 .+-. 0.0 to 1.1 .+-. 0.1 fmol .cntdot. cell-1 .cntdot. min-1 in the basal state and from 0.8 .+-. 0.1 to 5.5 .+-. 0.4 fmol .cntdot. cell-1 .cntdot. min-1 in the insulin-stimulated state in untreated and treated diabetic rats, respectively; this is a 3-fold increment of glucose transport rate in both states compared with control rats. After 14-day insulin therapy, glucose-transport  activity declined toward normal but still remained .apprx. 1.5- and 4-fold higher than control and diabetic rats, respectively. Despite the persistent enhancement of glucose transport rate, concentration of glucose transporters in the intracellular pool was restored only to its prediabetic state. Likewise, the increased concentration of glucose transporters in the plasma membranes after insulin stimulation was similar to that of control rats. Thus, we suggest that 8-14 days of insulin therapy reversed the insulin resistance in diabetic rat adipocytes by at least two mechanisms: restoration of the intracellular pool of glucose transporters and enhancement of glucose-transport activity. The mechanism(s) responsible for this supernormal glucose-transport activity is unknown but may be related to transient appearance of a factor coregulating cellular glucose transport and/or modulation of the intrinsic activity of the glucose transporter.

- temperature
- precipitation
- humidity
- wind
- drought
- heat
- cold
- other weather or climate conditions

C. Climate-related extreme events, such as:
- heatwaves
- floods
- droughts
- storms
- hurricanes/cyclones
- storm surges
- wildfires
- other climate-related hazards

D. Fossil fuels or fossil-fuel use, including:
- extraction
- production
- combustion
- consumption
- replacement
- their greenhouse-gas or other climate-forcing emissions (NOT non-climate combustion pollutants such as PAHs or heavy metals — see the air-pollution rule below)

E. Greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents, including:
- methane
- carbon dioxide
- nitrous oxide
- black carbon
- other recognized climate-forcing agents

F. An intervention or action that changes emissions of greenhouse gases or other climate-forcing agents.

A climate-related component is substantive when the climate-related factor, event, agent, or emission is:
- measured;
- analyzed;
- modeled;
- used as an exposure;
- used as an outcome;
- affected by an intervention; or
- otherwise important to the research question.

The climate-related component does NOT need to be the main topic of the paper.

For example:
- An animal nutrition study that evaluates methane emissions can have a climate-related component because methane is a climate-forcing agent.
- An air-pollution study can have a climate-related component when it studies a recognized climate-forcing pollutant/agent.
- A flood model can have a climate-related component when it studies a climate-related flood hazard.

DO NOT consider a record climate-related merely because climate change, temperature, fossil fuels, greenhouse gases, or another climate-related term appears incidentally in the background, introduction, discussion, or references.

IMPORTANT:
Air pollution in general is NOT automatically a climate-related component. The climate criterion is satisfied only when the pollutant is itself a relevant climate-forcing agent or the record explicitly connects the pollution to climate change.

IMPORTANT — INTENT:
A greenhouse gas, climate-forcing agent, or fossil-fuel substance makes a record climate-related ONLY when the study concerns it as a climate, energy, emissions, or air-quality matter. It does NOT qualify when the substance is present for an unrelated reason, e.g.: a greenhouse gas studied as a drug or toxicant (recreational nitrous-oxide abuse); a single fossil-fuel-derived chemical studied only for cellular/clinical toxicology (a diesel-exhaust compound tested in vitro); fossil-fuel infrastructure studied only as an industrial-accident or safety hazard (a pipeline explosion). The agent must be substantive to the research question as a climate/energy/emissions matter, not merely named.

--------------------------------------------------
2. QUALIFYING HEALTH COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The health pathway is satisfied when the record addresses human health or health systems, including:

- disease
- illness
- clinical symptoms
- morbidity
- mortality
- injury
- respiratory or cardiovascular health
- human exposure
- health risks
- occupational health
- public health
- healthcare
- health services
- health-system capacity, preparedness, resilience, or functioning

A record qualifies through the health pathway when the climate-related factor/event/agent/fossil fuel is studied in relation to human health or health systems.

Do NOT require a climate-related extreme event if a climate-forcing agent, fossil fuel, or other qualifying climate-related factor is directly related to human health.

For example:
A study measuring atmospheric pollutants and examining respiratory health can qualify through the climate + health pathway when the pollutants include relevant climate-forcing agents.

Do NOT infer human-health relevance merely because an environmental condition, pollutant, animal disease, agricultural outcome, or ecosystem change could theoretically affect human health.

INDIRECT HEALTH VIA CLIMATE EXPOSURE PATHWAYS (CCHE):
The health component is ALSO satisfied when the record substantively addresses a recognised climate-health exposure pathway through which climate/weather or a climate-forcing agent affects human health, even without a named clinical outcome. The recognised pathways are:
- Air quality (particulate matter, ground-level ozone, wildfire smoke/haze, pollen/aeroallergens, dust storms) -> respiratory/cardiovascular disease;
- Extreme weather events (floods, droughts, storms, storm surges, coastal flooding) -> injuries, fatalities, mental-health effects, health-care disruption;
- Food supply and safety / food security -> undernutrition, foodborne disease;
- Heat stress (heatwaves, cold spells, UV exposure) -> heat-related illness, skin/eye damage;
- Social factors (climate-driven displacement, migration, conflict) -> physical and mental-health effects;
- Vector distribution and ecology (mosquitoes, ticks, rodents, sandflies) -> vector-borne disease (malaria, dengue, Lyme, West Nile, etc.);
- Water quality and quantity (waterborne pathogens, HARMFUL ALGAL BLOOMS / cyanobacteria, drought- or flood-related contamination) -> cholera, cryptosporidiosis, diarrhoeal disease, etc.
A study of one of these exposures in a climate/weather or fossil-fuel/climate-forcing-agent context satisfies the health component through the indirect pathway. This does NOT override the guard above: a merely hypothetical or unstated health link still does not qualify -- the exposure pathway must be a substantive subject of the record.

--------------------------------------------------
3. QUALIFYING MITIGATION COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The mitigation pathway is satisfied when the record studies an action, intervention, technology, practice, policy, or management strategy that is intended to:

- reduce greenhouse-gas emissions;
- reduce another climate-forcing emission;
- remove greenhouse gases;
- reduce fossil-fuel use;
- replace fossil fuels;
- reduce dependence on fossil fuels; or
- otherwise mitigate climate change.

The record does not need to use the word "mitigation".

An intervention that directly changes or reduces emissions of a climate-forcing agent can qualify as mitigation even when the primary subject of the paper is something else.

For example:
A study of dietary sulphur in dairy cattle that examines effects on methane emissions can qualify because:
1. methane is a climate-forcing agent; and
2. an intervention affecting methane emissions constitutes a potential mitigation action.

Merely measuring methane, carbon dioxide, or another greenhouse gas does NOT by itself constitute mitigation.

The record must study an intervention, action, practice, technology, policy, or management approach that affects or is intended to affect emissions or fossil-fuel use.

IMPORTANT — A MITIGATION ACTION, NOT ENABLING RESEARCH:
The record must study, evaluate, or report the mitigation action itself — an intervention, measure, practice, policy, deployment, or management approach that reduces, or is intended to reduce, emissions or fossil-fuel use, or that upscales greenhouse-gas removals. Upstream, basic, or enabling research that merely relates to, characterises, or could inform a low-carbon technology — without itself studying an emission-reducing action or its effect on emissions or fossil-fuel use — does NOT qualify. For example: soil-physics, materials, or component modelling that "supports the design of" a geothermal or other renewable-energy system is enabling research, not a mitigation action; whereas evaluating a feed intervention that reduces methane emissions, or measures that cut a product's manufacturing emissions, IS a mitigation action.

--------------------------------------------------
4. QUALIFYING ADAPTATION COMPONENT
--------------------------------------------------

The adaptation pathway is satisfied when the record addresses:

- climate adaptation;
- preparedness;
- resilience;
- vulnerability reduction;
- climate-risk management;
- risk reduction;
- adaptation planning;
- preparation for climate-related hazards;
- response to climate-related hazards; or
- assessment of future climate-related risks for decision-making.

Adaptation does not have to mean an intervention that has already been implemented.

Research can qualify as adaptation-supporting research when it directly generates evidence needed for:
- adaptation planning;
- future projections;
- climate-risk assessment;
- preparedness;
- resilience planning;
- vulnerability assessment;
- hazard management; or
- risk reduction.

This includes relevant:
- models;
- datasets;
- experiments;
- projections;
- simulations;
- risk assessments;
- engineering studies;
- monitoring studies;
- decision-support tools.

For example:
A study modeling storm surges and compound coastal flooding can qualify if the study explicitly connects the results to future projections, prevention of flood risks, preparedness, resilience, or adaptation planning.

A study generating experimental data on storm surge, wave, or tsunami impacts on coastal structures can qualify when the research is directly relevant to assessment of coastal hazards, resilience, risk reduction, or adaptation planning.

IMPORTANT:
The exclusion for early-stage research applies primarily to immature mitigation/adaptation TECHNOLOGIES or INTERVENTIONS that are not ready for plausible real-world use.

Do NOT exclude ordinary scientific research, modeling, experiments, or data-generation merely because they are not themselves an implemented adaptation action.

The adaptation pathway requires the record to frame its purpose, explicitly or by direct inference, as informing human or societal climate adaptation, preparedness, resilience, or climate-risk management. The following do NOT qualify on their own: physiological/biological acclimation of organisms to temperature (the organism adapting is not climate-adaptation research); routine drainage, civil-engineering, or infrastructure studies with no stated climate-risk or adaptation purpose; descriptions of an ecosystem's protective function without a stated adaptation, risk-reduction, or resilience purpose. "Resilience", "vulnerability", or "adaptation" used in a biological or generic-engineering sense does not satisfy this pathway.

IMPORTANT -- ADAPTATION MUST PROTECT HUMAN HEALTH, HEALTH SYSTEMS, OR HUMAN-IMPORTANT ECOSYSTEMS:
The adaptation pathway is satisfied ONLY when the action or supporting research is intended to reduce the exposure or vulnerability of human health, health systems, or ecosystems of importance to humans (e.g. pollinators, protective or food-producing ecosystems) to actual or expected climate hazards -- typically a hazard that acts on humans through one of the recognised climate-health exposure pathways (air quality, extreme weather, food security, heat, social factors, vectors, water). Adaptation or resilience of purely physical, industrial, or economic assets with no human-health, health-system, or human-important-ecosystem target does NOT qualify. For example: protecting or optimising energy systems or industrial infrastructure against climate variability, or protecting land/soil from erosion, is out of scope unless the record connects it to human health, health systems, or a human-important ecosystem. Protecting human settlements or populations from coastal flooding, storm surge, or other extreme-weather hazards DOES qualify (extreme-weather exposure pathway).

--------------------------------------------------
5. STRENGTH OF THE CONNECTION
--------------------------------------------------

Distinguish between a substantive connection and a merely possible connection.

INCLUDE when the qualifying connection is:

A. EXPLICIT:
The abstract directly states the climate, health, mitigation, or adaptation relationship.

OR

B. DIRECTLY INFERABLE:
The relationship follows directly from what the study measures, evaluates, models, or changes.

For example:
- An intervention changes methane emissions -> mitigation is directly inferable.
- A climate-forcing pollutant is associated with respiratory symptoms -> climate + health is directly inferable.
- A coastal flood model is explicitly intended to inform future risk prevention -> adaptation relevance is explicit.

EXCLUDE when the connection is merely speculative or hypothetical.

For example:
- A generic environmental study that could potentially be useful for climate adaptation but does not indicate any adaptation, climate-risk, future-projection, resilience, or preparedness purpose.
- A pollutant study where the pollutant is not a climate-forcing agent and no climate connection is stated.
- A study of animal health where a human-health implication is merely possible.

--------------------------------------------------
6. ANIMAL STUDIES
--------------------------------------------------

Animal studies are not automatically excluded.

INCLUDE an animal study if it has a qualifying connection to:
- climate mitigation;
- climate adaptation;
- human food security; or
- human health.

Animal health alone is not equivalent to human health.

For example:
An animal nutrition study that evaluates methane emissions can qualify through the climate mitigation pathway even if it has no human-health outcome.

--------------------------------------------------
7. SEASONAL VARIATION
--------------------------------------------------

EXCLUDE records that report only normal seasonal variation without a connection to:
- climate change;
- altered or unusual patterns;
- climate variability;
- climate-related hazards;
- climate impacts;
- mitigation; or
- adaptation.

Do not exclude a record merely because it contains seasonal data if the study also addresses a qualifying climate-related question.

--------------------------------------------------
8. EXCLUSIONS
--------------------------------------------------

EXCLUDE records that:

1. Have no substantive climate-related component.

2. Have a climate-related component but no qualifying health, mitigation, or adaptation component.

3. Mention climate change, climate variables, fossil fuels, or climate-forcing agents only incidentally.

4. Concern normal seasonal variation without an altered, unusual, climate-change, climate-variability, mitigation, or adaptation component.

5. Describe subclinical outcomes that do not manifest as clinical symptoms, unless they are directly relevant to an otherwise qualifying human-health exposure or health risk.

6. Are animal studies with no qualifying climate mitigation, adaptation, human food-security, or human-health connection.

7. Describe an early-stage mitigation/adaptation technology or intervention with no plausible real-world application or deployment.

IMPORTANT:
Do not exclude a record merely because:
- climate change is not the primary topic;
- human health is not the primary topic;
- the study is environmental science, engineering, agriculture, animal science, hydrology, or air pollution research;
- the study is observational;
- the study is computational or modeling-based;
- the study generates experimental data;
- the adaptation action itself has not yet been implemented.

--------------------------------------------------
9. POSITIVE CALIBRATION EXAMPLES
--------------------------------------------------

Example 1:
"Significance of dietary sulphur and sulphate reducing bacteria in lactating dairy cattle"

Decision: INCLUDE

Reason:
The abstract discusses methane gas emissions in relation to an animal-nutrition intervention. Methane is a climate-forcing agent, and an intervention affecting methane emissions can constitute climate mitigation. The primary topic does not need to be climate change or human health.

Example 2:
"Acute effects of air pollution on respiratory health of 50-70 yr old adults"

Decision: INCLUDE

Reason:
The study measures atmospheric pollutants, including relevant climate-forcing pollutants, and directly examines respiratory health. This satisfies the climate + health pathway. A climate-related extreme event, mitigation action, or adaptation action is not additionally required.

Example 3:
"Impact of Tides and Surges on Fluvial Floods in Coastal Regions"

Decision: INCLUDE when the record explicitly connects the modeling to future projections, prevention of flood risks, preparedness, resilience, or adaptation planning.

Reason:
The study addresses a climate-related coastal flooding hazard and produces modeling evidence relevant to future risk management/adaptation. An implemented adaptation intervention is not required.

Example 4:
"Loading and Structural Response of Developed Shorelines Under Waves, Surge, and Tsunami Overland Flow Hazards"

Decision: INCLUDE when the record explicitly connects the research to coastal hazard assessment, risk reduction, resilience, preparedness, or adaptation planning.

Reason:
Experimental or data-generating research can qualify as adaptation-supporting research. The study does not need to implement an adaptation intervention or measure a health outcome.

--------------------------------------------------
10. FINAL DECISION
--------------------------------------------------

Before deciding, ask:

1. What is the substantive climate-related component?
2. Which qualifying pathway applies: health, mitigation, or adaptation?
3. Is that connection explicit or directly inferable from the study?
4. Is the connection substantive rather than merely incidental or hypothetical?

If the answer to question 1 is yes AND at least one qualifying pathway in question 2 is supported by the record, output:

INCLUDE

Otherwise output:

EXCLUDE

Return only the classification:

INCLUDE

or

EXCLUDE

document.name: A Comparative Analysis of Optimal Operation Scenarios in Hybrid Emission-Free Ferry Ships

content.abstract: The utilization of green energy resources for supplying energy to ships in the marine industry has received increasing attention during the last years, where different green resource combinations and control strategies have been used. This article considers a ferry ship supplied by fuel cells (FCs) and batteries as the main sources of ship's power. Based on the designers' and owners' preferences, different scenarios can be considered for managing the operation of the FCs and batteries in all-electric marine power systems. In this article, while considering different constraints of the system, six operating scenarios for the set of FCs and batteries are proposed. Impacts of each proposed scenario on the optimal daily scheduling of FCs and batteries and operation costs of the ship are calculated using a mixed-integer nonlinear programming model. Model predictive control (MPC) is also applied to consider the deviations from hourly forecast demand. Moreover, since the efficiency of FCs varies for different output powers, the impacts of applying a linear model for FCs' efficiency are compared with the proposed nonlinear model and its related deviations from the optimal operation of the ship are investigated. The proposed model is solved by GAMS software using actual system data and the simulation results are discussed. Finally, detailed real-time hardware-in-the-loop (HiL) simulation outcomes and comparative analysis are presented to confirm the adaptation capability of the proposed strategy.

document.name: Boosting Catalytic and Anti-fluorination Performance of the Ru/Vanadia–Titania Catalyst for the Oxidative Destruction of Freon by Sulfuric Acid Modification

content.abstract: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) exert a strong greenhouse effect and constitute the largest contributor to ozone depletion. Catalytic removal is considered an effective pathway for eliminating low-concentration CFCs under mild conditions. The key issue is the easy deactivation of the catalysts due to their surface fluorination. We herein report a comparative investigation on catalytic dichlorodifluoromethane (CFC-12) removal in the absence or presence of water over the sulfuric-acid-modified three-dimensionally ordered macroporous vanadia–titania-supported Ru (S-Ru/3DOM VTO) catalysts. The S-Ru/3DOM VTO catalyst exhibited high activity (T90% = 278 °C at space velocity = 40 000 mL g–1 h–1) and good stability within 60 h of on-stream reaction in the presence of 1800 ppm of water due to the improvements in acid site amount and redox ability that promoted the adsorption of CFC-12 and the activation of C–F bonds. Compared with the case under dry conditions, catalytic performance for CFC-12 removal was better over the S-Ru/3DOM VTO catalyst in the presence of water. Water introduction mitigated surface fluorination by the replenishment of hydroxyl groups, inhibited the formation of halogenated byproducts via the surface fluorine species cleaning effect, and promoted the reaction pathway of COX2 (X = Cl/F) → carboxylic acid → CO2.

- temperature
- precipitation
- humidity

- extraction
- production
- combustion

- replacement

- methane
- carbon dioxide
- nitrous oxide
- black carbon

- measured;
- analyzed;
- modeled;
- used as an exposure;
- used as an outcome;
- affected by an intervention; or

--------------------------------------------------

--------------------------------------------------

The health pathway is satisfied when the record addresses human health or health systems, including:

- disease
- illness
- clinical symptoms
- morbidity
- mortality
- injury
- respiratory or cardiovascular health
- human exposure
- health risks
- occupational health
- public health
- healthcare
- health services
- health-system capacity, preparedness, resilience, or functioning

- Heat stress (heatwaves, cold spells, UV exposure) -> heat-related illness, skin/eye damage;
- Social factors (climate-driven displacement, migration, conflict) -> physical and mental-health effects;
- Vector distribution and ecology (mosquitoes, ticks, rodents, sandflies) -> vector-borne disease (malaria, dengue, Lyme, West Nile, etc.);

document.name: In-flight fiber optic acoustic emission sensor (FAESense) system for the real time detection, localization, and classification of damage in composite aircraft structures

content.abstract: Acoustic emission sensing is a leading structural health monitoring technique use for the early warning detection of structural damage associated with impacts, cracks, fracture, and delaminations in advanced materials. Current AE systems based on electronic PZT transducers suffer from various limitations that prevent its wide dynamic use in practical avionics and aerospace applications where weight, size and power are critical for operation. This paper describes progress towards the development of a wireless in-flight distributed fiber optic acoustic emission monitoring system (FAESense™) suitable for the onboard-unattended detection, localization, and classification of damage in avionics and aerospace structures. Fiber optic AE sensors offer significant advantages over its counterpart electronic AE sensors by using a high-density array of micron-size AE transducers distributed and multiplex over long lengths of a standard single mode optical fiber. Immediate SHM applications are found in commercial and military aircraft, helicopters, spacecraft, wind mil turbine blades, and in next generation weapon systems, as well as in the petrochemical and aerospace industries, civil structures, power utilities, and a wide spectrum of other applications.

content.abstract: Abstract   High-purity H2 was produced by the sorption enhanced steam reforming (SESR) of acetic acid, a model compound of bio-oil obtained from the fast pyrolysis of biomass, in a fluidized bed reactor. A Pd/Ni–Co hydrotalcite-like material (HT) and dolomite were used as reforming catalyst and CO2 sorbent, respectively. The hydrogen yield and purity were optimized by response surface methodology (RSM) and the combined effect of the reaction temperature (T), steam-to-carbon molar ratio in the feed (steam/C) and weight hourly space velocity (WHSV) upon the sorption enhanced steam reforming process was analyzed. T was studied between 475 and 675 °C, steam/C ratio between 1.5 and a 4.5 mol/mol and WHSV between 0.893 and 2.679 h−1. H2 yield, H2 selectivity and H2 purity, as well as the CH4, CO and CO2 concentrations in the effluent gas, were assessed. The operating temperature proved to be the variable that had the greatest effect on the response variables studied, followed by the WHSV and the steam/C ratio. The results show that the H2 yield, H2 selectivity and H2 purity increased, while the CH4, CO and CO2 concentrations decreased, concurrently with the temperature up to around 575–625 °C. Higher values of the steam/C ratio and lower WHSV values favored the H2 yield, H2 selectivity and H2 purity, and reduced the CH4 concentration. It was found that the SESR of acetic acid at atmospheric pressure and 560 °C, with a steam/C ratio of 4.50 and a WHSV of 0.893 h–1 gave the highest H2 yield of 92.00%, with H2 purity of 99.53% and H2 selectivity of 99.92%, while the CH4, CO and CO2 concentrations remained low throughout (0.04%, 0.06% and 0.4%, respectively). document.name: Semi-automated BSM model building procedures in MARTY-1.1 through a 2HDM example

content.abstract: MARTY is a C++ computer algebra system specialized for High Energy Physics that can calculate amplitudes, squared amplitudes and Wilson coefficients in a large variety of beyond the Standard Model scenarios up to the one-loop order. It is fully independent of any other framework and its main development guideline is generality, in order to be adapted easily to any type of model. The calculations are fully automated from the Lagrangian up to the generation of the C++ code evaluating the theoretical results (numerically, depending on the model parameters). Once a phenomenological tool chain has been set up - from a Lagrangian to observable analysis - it can be used in a model independent way leaving only model building, with MARTY, as the task to be performed by physicists. Here we present the main steps to build a general new physics model, namely gauge group, particle content, representations, replacements, rotations and symmetry breaking, using the example of a 2 Higgs Doublet Model. The sample codes that are shown for this example can be easily generalized to any Beyond the Standard Model scenario written with MARTY.

INCLUDE
EXCLUDE

Base your decision only on the title, abstract, and other metadata provided. Do not use outside information to fill gaps in the record.

IMPORTANT:
- Do not require climate change, health, mitigation, or adaptation to be the primary topic of the paper.
- Do not require the paper to use the exact words "climate change", "mitigation", or "adaptation".

- Do not use an assumed prevalence of relevant records to make the decision.
- If the abstract is missing, very short, garbled, or otherwise incomplete, make the best decision possible from the available information.

CORE DECISION RULE

INCLUDE a record if it satisfies:

1. At least one substantive CLIMATE-RELATED component

AND

2. At least one qualifying HEALTH, MITIGATION, or ADAPTATION component.
